text: The director calls you in and offers a transfer to the international office abroad. Answer needed by Friday; tickets are already "sort of being looked at". Your answer?
The relocation manager sends a 40-item moving checklist. Item one: "Don't panic." Item two: "Gather certificates for the last ten years." Where do you start?
In the evening you tell Mom about the move. After a long silence she asks whether they have proper buckwheat "over there". Your answer?
Sveta heard about your move before you did: "I've already claimed your chair by the window, you don't mind, right?" You need the chair for two more weeks.
Accounting wants all your expense reports closed before you leave. You have eleven, and in three of them the receipts have faded to blank paper. What now?
The only consulate slot to hand in documents is at 7:15 a.m., across town. The next one is in a month. What do you do?
left: Get up at five and go

text: The work permit form asks you to "list every place you have visited in the last ten years". You only remember your summer cottage and the office.
right: Dig up all your old tickets

text: Packing night. The suitcase only closes if you and the cat sit on it together. The cat objects. What comes out?
HR asks you to sign a 14-page transfer addendum. At the bottom, in tiny print: "You undertake to learn the local language within three months."
right: Ask them to drop that clause

text: Your colleagues throw you a farewell. The cake has your name misspelled and a little flag of entirely the wrong country. Everyone tried so hard.
A childhood friend invites you to a farewell get-together on Friday. Your flight is at 6 a.m. Saturday. "Just for an hour!" he says. You know his hours.
Departure morning. Check-in says your bag is four kilos over. Inside: three kilos of documents and one kilo of Grandma's jam.
Your seatmate learns you're flying out for work and spends four hours explaining how "everything works there". He passed through once, back in 1998.
You land in the evening. The driver asks something in the local language. You confidently answer with a phrasebook line that, judging by his face, means "I am a potato."
right: Show the address on your phone

text: First morning in the temporary flat. The shower has three unlabelled levers. One of them seems to switch on the neighbours' heating.
right: Wash from the kettle and run

text: Reception at the new office hands you a badge with someone else's photo. "He's new too, you look alike," the receptionist smiles.
Ingrid, your new manager, opens with: "Which do you prefer — direct feedback, or very direct feedback?"
First lunch in the local canteen. The only thing on the counter you recognise is bread, and it's purple. The queue behind you waits politely.
Evening study with the phrasebook. Phrase number five: "My elephant has lost its luggage at the opera." So far there are fewer useful phrases than pages.
At the immigration office you get ticket no. 412. The screen shows 37. Next to you, a coffee machine with a sign: "Out of order since last year."
Mateo invites you for a "quick coffee" at 3 p.m. Turns out it's the whole team's daily 40-minute ritual, and talking shop is banned.
To open an account, the bank needs an address. To rent a flat, you need an account. To have an address, you need a flat. It's evening and the bank is closing.
left: Ask the company for a letter
right: Search forums for a way out

text: The alarm goes off at 7:00, but your body insists it's 4 a.m. Jet lag is winning. The meeting is at 9:30.
You message a colleague through a translator app: "Thanks, you really bailed me out." They reply with a confused emoji. The app wrote: "Thanks, you robbed me."
You call home at 8 p.m. It's 5 a.m. for your parents; Dad grabs the phone in a panic: "What happened?!" Nothing — you just miss them.
The meeting is set for 9:00. You walk in at 8:55; everyone's already seated, they started at 8:58. Here "on time" means "early".
Over lunch Aiko asks how to say "enjoy your meal" in your language. A week later the whole team says it with such an accent you no longer recognise it.
The agent sends a listing: "Cosy, bright, close to transport." In the photo, a tram passes about a metre from the window.
At the first lesson the teacher speaks only the local language. You catch your own name and, possibly, the word "homework".
A call with three offices in three time zones. Morning for some, night for others, lunch for you. Someone is chewing right into the mic, and it's you.
Evening at the supermarket: twenty minutes looking for milk. You've found five kinds of white bottles, each with a different animal on it, and not one cow.
The morning bus sails straight past your stop. Turns out you had to press a button on the pole. The next one is in twenty minutes.
Kwame moved here six months ago and offers you a "survival kit": the best spots, a handyman's number and the laundrette Wi-Fi password. In return he wants help with a presentation.
A friend video-calls to show everyone gathered at his cottage. "Shame you're not here!" Your favourite bench is in the background.
The printer menu is in the local language. You pressed the button that looked like "print". Now the printer is placing an order for cartridges.
The tax form asks for your "residency status". There are seven options, and by the descriptions you are both number three and number five.
At the viewing the landlord hands you six pages of house rules. Rule 14: "No vacuuming at weekends or after 7 p.m." It's 7:05.
Priya kindly warns you: here nobody agrees straight away in meetings — first you ask three questions. Yesterday you agreed to everything.
You arrive at the office and it's empty. It's a local holiday everyone knew about except you. The guard looks at you with sympathy.
Evening. You stand before six bins of different colours holding one bag with everything in it. A neighbour watches closely from her window.
At stand-up Ingrid says: "Your report's not bad, but the structure is weak, the conclusions are debatable and I dislike the font." Here, that counts as praise.
A parcel from home: a jar of pickles, sweets and a note from Mom. Customs opened it and added their own note: "The pickles are excellent."
Your temporary landlord reminds you to move out in a week. No permanent flat yet — just three "maybes".
The office coffee machine has a touchscreen in the local language. For three days you've been drinking hot milk. Colleagues walk by, oblivious to your plight.
Your cousin writes: "Since you're abroad now, bring me sneakers, headphones and this list." The list is two screens long, and your next trip home is in six months.
Your language class starts at 7 p.m., but at 6:30 Ingrid books a call "for half an hour". Her half-hours have never once ended on time.
Every morning Thomas greets you in your language — he learned it specially. Today, instead of "good morning", he confidently says "good night".
The visa centre wants a new photo: your smile is "unacceptably joyful". The photographer next door charges triple for urgency.
right: Ask a colleague to snap one

text: At 10 p.m. the downstairs neighbour knocks and explains something at length, pointing at the ceiling. You make out the word "water" and possibly "again".
In the morning your old office chat tags you twenty times: "Where's that file?" You handed everything over, but your successor is on holiday.
Fatima invites the whole team to dinner and asks everyone to bring a dish from home. Your repertoire is pasta with cheese and a sandwich.
You walk to work along a red path. A bell, a shout, and a cyclist whizzes past. The red path, it turns out, is not for pedestrians.
Ingrid asks you to run the weekly call with offices in three countries. The only time that suits everyone is 6:30 a.m. your time.
The basement laundry runs on a schedule. Your slot is Tuesday, 9–10 p.m. It's 9:50 and the machine is still spinning someone else's sheets.
At the morning meeting Jorge hugs everyone in turn. You haven't yet decided how greetings work in this office. He's coming your way.
Local HR sends a 30-page form. Half the questions are about your "family situation", and the field for your patronymic won't fit in the box.
At the viewing, the studio's bed folds out of a wardrobe and stops against the stove. The landlady says: "But everything's within reach!" Five others want it.
Morning call with head office. You're used to cameras on; here everyone's off. On screen there's only your face and a pastry.
Today the canteen serves fish soup with an unknown fish. The cook proudly describes it for three minutes. You catch only "tradition" and "eyes".
Mom wants to "see how you live" over video. She demands a tour of the fridge, the bathroom and your dinner. The fridge holds ketchup and one lonely egg.
Ngozi offers you a lift every morning: "It's on my way." But she leaves at 7:30, not at nine like you're used to.
After your question, the meeting falls silent for a long time. Back home this would mean "you said something dumb". Here, maybe, they're just thinking.
Grandma calls at 11 p.m. your time; it's already morning for her. She recaps a TV series you've never watched and checks you're eating properly.
Every morning the office guard says something to you and laughs. You laugh back. Today a colleague translated: he's asking why you never wear your badge.
At the review Yuki politely says: "Interesting approach." You're delighted, until Priya explains that here it means "redo everything".
Your second suitcase, shipped separately, arrives in the evening. Half of it is summer clothes, though you definitely packed winter ones. It's your old flatmate's bag.
right: Fight the courier for a week

text: A neighbour offers a language exchange: half an hour of his language, half an hour of yours. Saturdays at 8 a.m., "while the mind is fresh".
Oscar from accounting says your relocation allowance will be paid "next quarter". The deposit on the flat is due tomorrow.
Evening in your new, empty flat. The furniture arrives next week; for now there's a mattress, a lamp and a booming echo. The echo repeats your "oh well".
Lennart arrives an hour early and leaves at 4 p.m. sharp. You arrive at 10 and stay till eight. Ingrid asks why you keep "such an odd schedule".
In a meeting you try a phrasebook line to show effort. You're sure it means "great idea". Everyone goes quiet and, for some reason, looks at the window.
Your brother calls about his coursework. You've always helped him, but it's 10 p.m. and tomorrow is your first presentation in a foreign language.
In the office fridge every container is labelled with name and date. Your unlabelled lunch from yesterday has been neatly thrown out, with a note left behind.
Ingrid asks you to speak at the all-hands about "your relocation experience". So far your experience consists of six forms and one tram.
Your neighbour Gabriela brings you a pie "to welcome you". Rumour has it you're expected to bring something back within a week. You can't bake.
left: Buy a cake at a bakery

text: The immigration office rejects your certificate: the stamp is "not round enough". The officer suggests getting it certified again back home.
right: Request a new one from home

text: Samir asks you to translate an urgent client email into your language. Your own deadline is in an hour. "But you're a native speaker!"
In the evening you dash out for dinner and see the sign: shops here close at eight. It's 8:02. At home there's only tea.
Annika offers to be your "buddy": she'll answer any question about the country. Your first question: why does everyone here eat soup for breakfast?
On the international video call the audio lags five seconds. You and someone from another office have said "no, you go first" at the same time three times now.
Your new landlady sent a 12-page radiator manual in the local language. It's +5°C outside, and +5°C inside.
Colleagues run along the embankment at 7 a.m. on weekends and invite you. Usually you only run for the bus.
In a meeting Bruno loudly disagrees with Ingrid. You're used to that being unthinkable and shrink. Ingrid thanks Bruno and asks your opinion.
At the post office you collect Mom's parcel. The duty costs more than the contents: woollen socks, bread rings and a photo of the cat.
IT hands you a laptop with a local keyboard layout. The keys aren't where fifteen years of habit put your fingers. Ingrid needs an email by lunch.
Zeynep explains that here you celebrate your own birthday by treating everyone yourself. Your birthday is tomorrow.
A ticket inspector boards the evening tram. Your ticket turns out to be a child fare: you pressed the machine button whose icon looked like a little person with a briefcase.
Arjun writes in the team chat in six languages, switching mid-sentence. You understand every sixth word. He asks if you agree.
The insurance company wants your childhood vaccination record. Mom found it, but it's written in handwriting no one on earth could read.
Hana invites you to a local concert tonight. You're tired, but it's your first non-work invitation in a month.
In the morning Ingrid writes: "Got five minutes?" Back home, that meant you were about to be fired. Here she just has a question about your leave.
Meetings here are held standing up to keep them short. Today's standing meeting is now in its second hour.
In the evening the building chat debates who left a bike in the hallway. It's not yours, but everyone writes in a language you don't speak.
In the morning you ride the metro the wrong way — the map here spirals. Twenty minutes later you're at the terminus by the sea.
right: Snap a photo of the sea

text: Elsa suggests sharing a desk by day: Mondays and Wednesdays are yours. Today is Tuesday, and all your papers are on her side.
Sunday evening. You found a video of your home street online and are watching it for the fifth time. You have to be up early tomorrow.
right: Call a colleague for a walk

text: Tariq posts in the team chat: "Who can stand in for me at a conference tomorrow? It's in another city, 6 a.m. train." Ingrid likes your message, though you haven't written anything yet.
A friend from home calls to vent about her boss. As you listen, you realise you miss even that boss.
Your morning train is cancelled; the announcement is only in the local language. Everyone heads confidently for a bus. You follow everyone.
Procurement sent you a supplier form in the local language, marked "urgent". You translated the first line: "Please take your time."
You're buying a local SIM in the morning. The seller offers twelve plans, all named after birds. "Sparrow" is cheaper; "Eagle" includes calls home.
A client in another time zone asks to move the call to "your morning". His morning is your midnight, and he seems blissfully unaware.
A great flat, cheap, near a park. One condition: the landlady's cat stays with you — "he'll decide himself when to leave".
At the partner meeting everyone ceremoniously swaps business cards with both hands. Yours are in another country, in a desk drawer.
Mei explains that in the canteen you take a tray from one side and return it on the other, and it matters a lot. You've been doing it backwards for two weeks.
Your sister sends a photo of family dinner: everyone at the table, your chair empty except for your portrait propped on it. "So it's like you're here."
right: Have a little cry and sleep

text: Ingrid cancels the morning meeting: "No agenda, no meeting." Back home, agenda-less meetings ran for three hours.
A business lunch. The partners spend half an hour on weather, kids and gardens. You wait for the contract talk to begin. Dessert arrives.
Your online order went to a pickup point across town. Open till 7 p.m. It's 6:20.
Karim brought sweets to celebrate his holiday and is offering them around. You don't know which holiday it is and fear congratulating him wrongly.
You pitch an idea at the meeting. Everyone nods, says "interesting" and moves on. A month later Bruno pitches the same idea and everyone loves it.
It's your best friend's birthday. The party is 3,000 km away; you're on a tablet in the corner. An hour later, they forget to switch you off.
Sideways freezing rain this morning. Local colleagues cycle in, thrilled. You arrive soaked through and in despair.
Oscar explains the expense process: receipt, translation of the receipt, signature, and a photo of the receipt next to your face. You spent six euros on a taxi.
left: Do it all by the book

text: In class the teacher asks you to describe your hobby. You know the words "work", "coffee" and "sleep". Honestly, that is your hobby.
Samir asks why you never smile in meetings. You do smile. That's just how serious people smile where you're from.
A two-hour conference in English with seven different accents. You speak after someone who talks very fast and very quietly.
At 10 p.m. the landlady texts: "A technician is coming to read the meter tomorrow at 8. You'll be home, right?" Tomorrow at 8 you're on a plane for work.
Every morning the receptionist pronounces your name differently. Today it sounds like a type of cheese. You kind of like it.
Local cuisine day in the canteen. The dish of the day is a single word your translator app renders as "Grandma's surprise".
In the evening you scroll old photos and find one from your first day at the old job. You didn't understand anything back then either, and it turned out fine.
Gabriela turns out to be both your neighbour and a colleague from the next department. In the lift this morning she asks about her pie dish.
Ingrid asks why you haven't taken a single day off in three months. "Here it looks as if you're not coping."
The wardrobe arrived in 84 pieces with a picture-only manual. The little man in the pictures is smiling. You are not.
The light at an empty crossing is red. Not a car in sight. The locals stand and wait; you're late for a meeting.
Niko kindly points out that people here sign emails "Warmly", while you write "Respectfully". He thinks you're upset with everyone.
Every night at ten the upstairs neighbours move furniture. Apparently it's a hobby here. You've an early call with the home office.
The office has an anonymous suggestion box. You'd like to propose labelling the coffee machine in several languages but fear looking fussy.
On a call with your old team, you catch yourself speaking your own language with an accent. Your ex-boss laughs: "Totally a foreigner now!"
You found a shop selling food from home. Prices are like a jeweller's: a packet of biscuits costs as much as a canteen lunch.
You got a badge, but your department's doors need a second badge, ordered through a system that requires a badge. Colleagues have been letting you in for a week.
Jorge suggests running a project together. He's great fun and very unreliable: deadlines, to him, are "a mood".
In the evening you add a second clock to your phone showing home time. Now every time you see it, you think everyone at home is asleep.
HR wants an address confirmation by post. You have a mailbox, but it still bears the last tenant's name, so the postman takes everything back.
right: Ask to send it to the office

text: At an international conference someone asks a question after your talk in such complex English that all you understand is "thank you".
right: Answer a question of your own

text: Kwame suggests a weekend trip out of town: "The best cure for homesickness." Leaving at 6 a.m., and bring a tent.
A 7 a.m. call with an office on another continent. You join washed and in a shirt. Everyone else is in pyjamas with cats.
Leila asks if you like the city. You honestly say you miss home. She goes quiet, then brings you a catalogue of local hobby clubs.
Your first electricity bill arrives, three times what you expected: you've spent a month heating the flat with the last tenant's ancient heater.
You order coffee near the office in the local language. The barista replies in your own language because he "heard the accent". You'd practised that line for a year.
left: Keep going in the local one

text: Ingrid asks not to be copied on emails: "If I'm in cc, it means you don't trust your colleagues." Back home you cc'd the boss just in case.
At the evening market a vendor offers you cheese that smells like an old gym. Declining, they say, is rude.
Hana asks why you're so glum this morning. Yesterday was your dad's birthday and you were on a call and missed ringing him.
Ingrid needs a report for head office in the local language. Your level is "order coffee and apologise".
In the evening a waiter asks "Table for one?" so loudly the whole room turns. It's the third time this week you've dined alone.
A letter from the immigration office arrives. Inside: one sentence of legalese and a phone number nobody answers.
Elsa asks you to join the office choir. Rehearsals are Wednesday lunchtimes. You sing only in the shower, and only one song.
Mom is worried: the parcel with your winter boots was returned to sender. The reason is in the local language. You translate: "Boots too warm."
Olusegun arrives at 9:00 sharp and is always surprised you've been in since eight. "Do you live here?" Half the team laughs.
The company runs a mandatory local-language test. Question one is listening: a recording of someone who, by the sound of it, is driving through a tunnel.
On Monday morning Ingrid asks, "How was your weekend?" and actually waits for details. You slept all weekend and watched videos from home.
Bruno loudly discusses salaries with you in the open-plan office. It's normal here; your ears are burning with embarrassment.
The eighth viewing this week. The flat is perfect, but there are forty applicants and the owner wants a "motivation letter about yourself".
Morning in the team chat: "Who took my mug with the cat?" The cat mug is on your desk. You thought it was communal.
HR reminds you your work permit expires in a month, while renewal takes two. The renewal documents, naturally, need an apostille.
Mom is thrilled: she's mastered video calls and now rings every evening at 9 p.m. Tonight you're at dinner with colleagues.
You bought a bike like everyone else. On the way in you learn that cyclists signal turns with hand gestures. You signalled something odd, and people are honking.
Yuki gives you a little gift "for your first month". You don't know if you're meant to open it in front of the giver. She's watching expectantly.
left: Open it in front of her
right: Tuck it away with a bow

text: Friday evening. Colleagues are heading out, but you want to go home, crawl under a blanket and watch a show in your own language, no subtitles.
The stand-up is in the local language, though everyone knows you don't speak it yet. Ingrid asks: "Any questions?" You don't even know the topic.
Lunch here is an hour and everyone leaves the building. You're used to eating at your desk. Ingrid stares at your container by the keyboard in horror.
left: Go out to lunch with all

text: Your tap starts leaking in the evening. The plumber can't come for two weeks, but your neighbour says she can fix it, in exchange for a lesson in your language for her kids.
The courier left a note: "You were not home." You were, but the intercom here chirps like a bird and you didn't realise it was the doorbell.
left: Camp by the door all day

text: Ingrid offers you flexible hours: work whenever suits you. Puzzled, you ask who'll check on you. "You will," she says.
A friend texts: "So how's life abroad? Must be a party every day?" You're sitting in an empty flat eating cereal for dinner.
Karim asks how to address you: here everyone uses first names, but you signed your report with your full name and patronymic.
You're put on a project with an office whose workday starts as yours ends. Handovers happen through notes in a shared doc.
Your old neighbour rings to say the cat you left with Mom has learned to open the fridge. Mom is delighted; the fridge less so.
right: Send the cat a video hello

text: Oscar teaches you a local morning greeting. A week later you find out it's a football chant from his home neighbourhood.
Priya explains that here you close your laptop when someone comes to talk. You're used to typing and nodding at the same time.
The postman left a neighbour's parcel with you. The neighbour knocks and thanks you profusely. A week later there are six strangers' parcels at your door.
In the morning you sit the language exam for your visa. The examiner asks about your favourite dish. All you remember is the word "soup".
right: Admit it, ask for the word

text: Ngozi asks you to cover for her on a call while she picks up her child. It's with a client you know only by name.
Colleagues invite you to a festive dinner in the local tradition. The dish takes six hours and everyone helps. You know how to slice bread.
Ingrid asks your opinion on the new strategy and adds: "Honestly, please, even if it's bad." She wrote the strategy.
The partner office sent a one-sentence email with no greeting. You're offended. Priya laughs: "That means they already like you."
You're finally offered a flat. The owner wants to sign tonight at 11 p.m. across town because he "flies out in the morning".
Every morning at 8:00 Sun-mi leads a five-minute stretch for the team. You're shy and hide behind your monitor. She's heading your way.
Your ex-boss asks you, "as an old friend", to do a report for your old team. Ingrid doesn't know about this side job.
Dad asks to see "where you live now". You pan the camera round the room and he spots dust on the wardrobe through the screen.
In the morning reception asks you to sign in a guest on the terminal in the local language. You accidentally register him as a pizza courier.
The team heads to a local restaurant. The menu has no pictures. Everyone recommends something different, and each tip sounds like a dare.
Winter here means plus ten and rain. You miss snow so much you open the freezer just to look at the frost.
Rafael constantly interrupts in meetings, affectionately. Here it shows interest. You keep waiting for a pause to get a word in, but there are no pauses.
The company lawyer says that to extend your visa you must show "ties to the region". He suggests joining a local club.
A friend from home is visiting your city for three days, sure you'll show her everything. You only know the way from home to the office.
On the morning bus everyone is silent. Totally. You reply to Mom's voice message, and the whole bus looks at you reproachfully.
right: Get off and finish the call

text: Mateo asks why you're always apologising. This morning you've said sorry eleven times, once to a chair.
The neighbours start drilling at 8 p.m. Noise is allowed until ten here. You have a 9 p.m. call with the home office.
left: Take the call over the drill
right: Take the laptop to a café

text: Morning, rain, and you forgot your umbrella. Colleagues say nobody here carries one — "that's for tourists". Everyone's wet and happy.
Ingrid offers you company-paid language lessons, during work hours. That's two hours a day struck from your schedule.
right: Study on your own at night

text: You eat dinner at eight; your local colleagues eat at six or ten. At eight every restaurant is empty and the waiter eyes you like a riddle.
Annika asks why your desk has nothing personal — no photos, no plants. "It's like you're about to leave."
Mom rings: her TV won't work and only you know how to switch the input. You're in a meeting with Ingrid.
For the first time you decide to just wander the new city in the evening. An hour later you're lost and your phone's dead.
A memo arrives: "Reminder: the office is closed tomorrow for the plant inventory." You don't know what that means, but it sounds serious.
Leila takes you to a tiny local café with a menu only in the local language. "You order yourself, I won't help," she smiles.
Your last evening in the temporary flat. The landlord wants it back "in the same condition". The shower lever that heated the neighbours is somehow in your suitcase.
Tariq offers a swap: he takes your early call, you take his late one. Early is 6:30 a.m., late is 10 p.m. You're a night owl, but this morning you feel unusually perky.
Your nephew wants help with homework over video. It's 8 p.m. for him, midnight for you. The problem is about two trains heading towards each other.
You've been given a parking space, but you don't have a car. Colleagues hint it could go to someone who commutes from far away.
Marketing wants you in a video, "Our International Office". You must say one line in the local language. It's take nineteen.
Grandma sent a nine-minute voice message. Half is a pie recipe, the other half a list of neighbours who asked about you.
Hot water in the new flat runs out after four minutes. The neighbour says it's designed that way to save energy. Your usual shower takes fifteen.
The clocks went back here overnight, but not at home. You show up an hour early to the home-office call and sit in an empty room.
left: Wait and get some work done

text: Jorge brings his dog in — allowed here on Fridays. The dog picks your desk and lies on your feet all day.
right: Ask him to take it back

text: In the shop your home bank card gets blocked: "suspicious activity abroad". No local card yet, and dinner's in the basket.
left: Call the bank from the queue

text: Ingrid announces no one answers emails after 6 p.m. At all. At 6:05 you reply to a client out of habit. Ingrid sees.
You set a meeting for 03.04, meaning the third of April. Here that's the fourth of March. The partners showed up a month ago, and you weren't there.
At the supermarket you hear your own language: a woman at the till talking to her child. You want to hug her, but that might be weird.
Samir asks why you write "ok" in chat with no emoji. He thinks you're angry. You're just saving time.
It's vegetarian day in the canteen. The burger tastes like a burger, but the ingredients list says only mushroom and hope.
Out with colleagues. The bill comes and everyone pulls out phones to pay their exact share to the cent. Back home you'd treat everyone or split evenly.
First morning in your permanent flat. Quiet, light, your own mug. But the internet comes in three weeks and your call is in an hour.
Annika invites you to a "walking meeting" — discussing the project while circling the block. It's windy and drizzling.
Your sister's had a baby, and you're the last to know: thanks to the time difference, all the news arrives while you're asleep.
Today you're collecting your residence card. The officer asks if you want the photo "as is" or retaken. In the "as is", your eyes are shut.
The meeting-room voice assistant can't parse your accent. You ask it to "turn on the projector"; it books a taxi to the airport.
First visit to a board-game club. The rules are explained in the local language, fast and full of jokes. You smile just in case.
Ingrid offers to move you from the open plan into an office, on one condition: the door stays open. The draught and every conversation are now yours.
Ngozi asks you to say a few words about your country at a presentation. You're afraid of clichés and don't know where to begin.
The landlady sends the water bill, politely amazed at your usage. Locals shower four times faster, "on average", she writes.
Everyone at the meeting drinks something green and healthy. You turn up with a triple espresso and a sticky bun. Someone whispers: "Brave."
On a five-office call, a rooster crows behind one participant. Everyone pretends not to hear. The rooster crows right in your slot.
Friday evening Kwame texts: "Tomorrow, seven, station, bring sandwiches." You never agreed to any hike, but apparently you're going.
Lennart asks you to stop emailing him at weekends. You haven't. Your email settings just still have your old time zone.
IT switches every program's interface to the local language "for immersion". You spend an hour finding "Save". It looks just like "Delete".
Your old colleagues ring from their office party: "Say a few words!" You're on the other side of the world, it's midnight, and you've a call at seven.
You learn this morning that here the week starts on Sunday, so your weekly report is a day late.
Hana teaches you how to eat a local dish properly. Turns out for three months you've been eating the wrapper and leaving the filling.
Sunday evening. Every shop here closes on Sundays and you forgot to stock up. The fridge holds mustard and hope.
Priya brings a cake: the anniversary of her move to this country. She says she cried in the lift for the first six months. You cried in the lift yesterday.
Ingrid asks you to write a "culture guide" for newcomers from your country. You've only been here three months and learned half the rules by breaking them.
Mom sent sweets "for your colleagues, so they'll like you". There are twenty sweets and forty colleagues.
right: Give them to your team only

text: Ingrid invites you for a one-to-one morning coffee. You braced for a talk about mistakes; she just asks how you're sleeping.
Sales wants you to visit a client and "charm him with your accent". You're not sure if that's a compliment.
Your language app pings: "You've missed 14 days. The owl is sad." You're tired and sad too.
In the morning the door slams shut with your keys inside. The locksmith says something fast and long on the phone. You catch a number, and it's scary.
Thomas offers you half his tasks while he's on holiday. In exchange he promises to show you "the secret spot with the best pastries".
First trip to a local cinema. The film is dubbed into the local language, no subtitles. You do recognise the actors.
At the morning video meeting, auto-captions translate your speech live. Your "let's think about it" became "let's blow on it".
Oscar says the company won't pay for your business trip home because you were "most likely visiting your mother". You did, in fact, visit your mother.
In the evening rain a cycle courier splashes you and shouts "Sorry!" in your own language. He's from your home town.
Colleagues discuss local news in the morning. You don't know a single name in it, but everyone looks at you, awaiting an opinion.
You booked a meeting room for the whole day, not knowing it's frowned upon here. A note on the door: "Someone very important?"
Gabriela brought food again and left her containers again. Half your kitchen is now her tupperware. You're meant to return them full.
right: Return them empty with a card

text: Ingrid asks if you'd be ready to lead a team in this office in a year. You still can't operate the local cash machine.
Zeynep suggests co-presenting at the internal conference: "Working across time zones without losing your mind." You're unsure about part two.
Mom asks when you're coming back. You don't know yourself. The contract's two years, but some colleagues have been here ten.
You cycle in and the rack is full. There are more bike spots than car spaces, and still none free.
A client on the phone speaks a local dialect so fast your translator app gives up. He seems happy, but you can't be sure.
You try Grandma's soup with local ingredients. Everything is similar but not quite. The result is something else entirely, but still tasty.
right: Eat it alone, shed a tear

text: The train is three minutes late and the carriage is full of heavy sighs. Back home three minutes wouldn't even register.
Each quarter colleagues write anonymous feedback on each other. About you there's one line: "Works too much. Make them rest."
Evening: your first local tax return. The website logs you out every ten minutes and won't save drafts. Deadline is tomorrow.
Bruno starts the morning with a 40-minute debate on how to brew tea properly. You're no longer sure who's right. Work has stalled.
You're coordinating a project with people in six countries. Everyone's holidays differ; the calendar has no single day when all are working.
Your neighbour practises the trumpet every evening. Noise is allowed till 10 p.m. here. He plays till 9:59 and not a minute longer.
Dad rings: his phone broke and he's calling from the neighbour's. The neighbour also wants to say hi and ask about the weather.
Aiko brings a lunch that scents the whole floor. Others wrinkle their noses, but you like it. She offers you a taste in front of everyone.
left: Taste it in front of all

text: Ingrid invites you to dinner at her home. You don't know what to bring: flowers? A cake feels awkward. Maybe nothing?
HR asks if you want your surname in the local transliteration. In the old version nobody can read it; in the new one, you can't.
For an entire call, someone from another office calls you by your predecessor's name. You never corrected him, and now it's too late.
The corner shop owner knows you now and saves your favourite bread. Today he asks why you look so sad.
Mateo greets everyone each morning with two cheek kisses. You still can't work out which side to start on, and yesterday you bumped noses.
Ingrid asks you to interview a candidate in the local language. You understand about 40% of his answers, and he seems to get about the same of your questions.
You put a plant on your windowsill to feel at home. Next day the neighbours put out plants too. You seem to have started a contest.
You accidentally sit in the quiet carriage and answer a call. An elderly lady silently points to the sign with a crossed-out phone.
Olusegun offers to teach you local swear words "just in case". You're scared of using them wrongly, but it's hilarious.
Your ex-boss writes: "How's it going? Fancy coming back? A position's opened up." It's midnight and you've had a rough day.
Sun-mi suggests switching to the informal "you" in work emails. Your language has no such distinction; the local one has three. You're unsure which one she meant.
At the canteen till you're asked for your staff discount card. You've been paying full price for three months because you didn't know it existed.
right: Get the card, let it go

text: Friends on a video call discuss mutual acquaintances and new in-jokes you don't get. You laugh on a delay, like on an international call.
Ingrid brings you to a leadership meeting. Everyone sits on gym balls. You sit, and your ball slowly rolls towards the window.
To register with a local clinic you need a twelve-page form. Question nine: "How do you usually cope with stress?"
You watch a local TV series to learn the language. The plot escapes you, but you're deeply invested in the grandma from episode three.
An email from someone in another office: "As agreed, expecting it by lunch." You agreed to nothing. Probably.
Rafael invites you to a relative's wedding. You've known him two weeks and have no idea what to give or wear.
House rules ban drying laundry on the balcony. There's no dryer in the flat. Your living room looks like a sailing ship.
Niko asks if he can photograph your lunch for his blog about colleagues' food. Today it's buckwheat and a sausage.
At the meeting a partner praises your work at length, then says "but". After the "but" come twenty minutes of criticism. You no longer remember the praise.
In language class you're paired with a pensioner learning "for the grandkids". His homework beats yours, and he brings biscuits.
You learn this morning that the office uses commas, not points, for decimals. Your spreadsheet shows a profit a thousand times too big.
Fatima notices you've stopped joining the group lunch. She asks if you're OK and offers to have lunch together, just the two of you.
Your brother rings to say he got into university. You celebrate so loudly the neighbour bangs on the wall: it's 10:01 p.m.
Ingrid lets you work from home two days a week. It's quiet, but in three days you've talked to no one except the courier.
A delegation from your home country is visiting. You're appointed interpreter, though you still mix up local words.
It's Mom's birthday. Sending flowers to your home town from abroad costs as much as a plane ticket.
The barista by the office has memorised your order and now says it in your language, with a terrible accent. The whole café turns round.
Tariq proposes a skill swap: you teach him reports, he teaches you how to talk to local clients. Fridays after work.
Residents here take turns cleaning the stairwell. Yours was yesterday, and there's already a polite note on your door with an exclamation mark.
You propose a solution and everyone agrees at once. Suspicious. Priya later explains: they all just wanted lunch.
You're sent on a trip to a neighbouring country: another language, another currency, differently shaped sockets. You forgot your adapter.
At 11 p.m. a message from an office on another continent: "Urgent, the server's down." Your workday ended five hours ago.
right: Pass it to the on-call person

text: The bank's morning queue runs on tickets. Yours was skipped while you puzzled over a blinking word on the screen.
HR invites you to an "integration meeting". You expect paperwork; instead there's a counsellor, a soft sofa and the question: "How are you feeling here?"
The neighbours throw a courtyard party and invite you. Everyone brings something and talks about themselves for a minute. In the local language.
right: Drop off a cake and leave

text: Elsa asks you to check her slides in your language for the delegation. The title reads not "welcome" but "well, go away".
Ingrid catches you working through lunch again and confiscates your laptop for an hour: "Go outside. That's an order."
For the first time you dream in the local language, fluently. In the morning you can't recall a word, but you feel great.
There's a transport strike this morning that everyone knew about from the local news. You don't read the local news and stand at an empty stop.
Jorge forgot a deadline and asks you to cover for him with Ingrid: "Say we're finishing it together." It's the first you've heard of the task.
In the evening you catch yourself converting every price into your home currency. An apple costs a lunch back home. You've been at the stall ten minutes.
Ingrid makes a joke in the morning meeting and everyone laughs. You laugh a second later, after your neighbour whispers the translation. Ingrid notices and laughs again — kindly, at you.
Ingrid tells you you're being moved onto a project run from another continent. Meetings at 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. your time.
Leila asks why you always say "fine" when asked how you are. Here "fine" sounds like "everything is terrible".
You cooked dinner for one and caught yourself telling the saucepan about your day. The saucepan listens better than some colleagues.
The immigration officer praises your form: "Perfectly filled in." Then it turns out you completed the student form.
The other office asks for the work "by end of day". You send it at 6 p.m. your time, while it's still morning there. They're amazed at your speed.
You joined the local chat for people from your country. 800 members, all discussing where to buy sour cream. You want to know too.
On a call you're asked to introduce yourself. You do it in the local language, rehearsed ten times. Everyone claps. Turns out they were all calling from your home country.
right: Carry on in the local one

text: Ingrid asks why you're silent in meetings. Back home the most senior spoke and others listened. Here silence reads as having no opinion.
The landlady announces a rent rise from the new year. Local law says three months' notice. She gave three days.
Samir asks you to mentor him — he's preparing to relocate to another country too. You've barely settled in yourself.
Today's canteen soup comes in a bread bowl. You eat the soup and politely leave the bread. The cook looks at you as if you'd left the plate.
A friend sent you a box of "childhood flavours": biscuits, soda, processed cheese. Customs sent it back because of the cheese.
The bus driver greets every passenger and each one replies. You're too slow, so he repeats it just for you.
Ngozi asks you to help her child's school project: "Tell him about your country, he needs an interview." It's on Saturday.
A friend from home suggests a call on Saturday at 3 p.m. "my time". You calculate three times and get either 10 a.m. or tomorrow.
The budget meeting is in local currency. You mentally convert each figure to your home currency and panic at every number.
Ingrid offers to send you to a conference on the other side of the world. The flight's in three days; that visa takes a week.
You walk home with no umbrella, like the locals taught you. Tonight it's pouring, and somehow every local has an umbrella.
right: Wait it out in a café

text: Lennart proposes the team start each morning with five minutes of silence. You're used to starting with twenty messages and mild panic.
On an international video conference the interpreter goes on lunch break. Forty minutes of discussion in three languages remain.
The flat's washing machine breaks. The repairman asks you to describe the fault in the local language. You know "water", "noise" and "sad".
A letter from the tax office arrives. Your translator app renders it as "Congratulations, you owe." No amount given.
Arjun invites you to his family celebration: a hundred people, dancing and food till dawn. Tomorrow your report is due to Ingrid.
Mom rings to say she's turning your old room into a study for Dad. "You're not coming back anyway." You haven't decided that yet.
Your new desk neighbour eats tinned sardines for breakfast. In an open-plan office. At 8:30 a.m.
HR reminds you about the compulsory "Workplace Cultural Norms" course. You take the test and fail the question about greetings.
You agreed to have dinner with your family over video at the same time: 7 p.m. Their 7 p.m., that is — midnight for you.
Hana suggests a team tradition: every Monday someone talks about their country. She nominates you to go first.
A local client asks where you're from and spends twenty minutes on his holiday in your country. The agenda waits.
You find a note from the previous tenant: "If the upstairs neighbour drums, knock three times with a mop. It's a code." The neighbour is drumming.
The office is 18°C in the morning "for economy and ecology". The locals wear T-shirts. You're in your coat with a flask.
Thomas asks you to check his email to a client in your language. It opens "Dear comrade" and signs off "Kisses".
The news back home reports a big snowfall. Mom rings to say it's knee-deep. You stare enviously at the rain outside.
A courier brings your documents from the consulate but will only hand them over against your passport. Your passport is at the consulate.
Ingrid asks why you didn't take sick leave when you were coughing across the office yesterday. Here working while ill is considered rude.
right: Finish the day in a mask

text: Evening attempt at a regulation ID photo: no smile, no glasses, ears visible. Your ears are hidden under your hair.
A newcomer from yet another country joins the team. Ingrid asks you to look after him. You remember getting lost on your own first day.
A colleague from another office says "Good!" in your language on a call. He learned it for you and now answers every question with it.
For the first time in a month, you're doing nothing in the evening. Guilt nags: maybe you should study, answer emails or call Mom.
Something is announced over the office tannoy and everyone starts leaving. You catch only the word "fire", or maybe "breakfast".
Gabriela asks you to take in her parcel while she's away. It turns out to be a two-metre sofa. Your flat is twenty square metres.
An acquaintance from home offers evening translation work. Good money, but your contract requires Ingrid's consent for side jobs.
Ingrid holds a meeting with no chairs, laptops or phones. Everyone stands in a circle. Your phone buzzes in your pocket — it's Mom.
Your language teacher asks you to sing at the school party. You know one local song, and it's about potatoes.
At 10 p.m. Ingrid writes: "Can you run tomorrow's meeting in the local language? You speak it well now." You only speak it well in your head.
Ingrid invites you for a pre-work morning run: "The best decisions come on the move." You haven't run since school and doubt any decisions can keep up.
Priya is burning out: doing two people's work and crying in the meeting room. Ingrid is on holiday. Priya asks you not to tell anyone.
New Year's Eve. Home celebrates four hours earlier, so you toast the family on video at 8 p.m. By local midnight you're nodding off.
You were five minutes late. Nobody said a word, but on your desk lies a printout: "Punctuality is respect", with a cute kitten.
right: Pin the kitten above your desk

text: The bank finally opens your account, but posts the card in the previous tenant's name, because that's what the mailbox says.
right: Wait for the tenant to forward it

text: You decide to bring your cat over. He needs a passport, a microchip, a certificate and a carrier of "approved size". So far the cat approves of none.
left: Do it all for the cat

text: Your shipping container is stuck in customs. They want an inventory in the local language: every spoon and every book listed separately.
Zeynep says her first six months abroad at her last job were hard too. She suggests a weekly lunch to moan to each other.
Your parents want to visit for two weeks. Your studio has one bed, and those two weeks are quarterly report time.
You run the morning meeting in the local language for the first time. You stumble on "quarter" and Lennart gently prompts you. Everyone waits.
left: Carry on in the local one

text: Your work permit is renewed, but there's a typo in your date of birth. On paper you're 112 years old.
People from your home country invite you to a meetup. Everyone moans about the locals, the weather and the food. Suddenly you want to defend this city.
Bruno walks in and says: "Your presentation yesterday was boring." No softening. Then he offers to help improve it.
You're hosting a four-country call. One office hears but can't see you; another sees but can't hear; the third dropped off. The fourth is Ingrid.
Your old neighbour is visiting your city and bringing "a parcel from Mom". It's a 23-kilo suitcase, and he's dragging it across town.
right: Ask him to leave it at the door

text: In the café by the office the locals queue in total silence. Out of habit you ask, "Who's last?" Everyone stares, puzzled.
IT asks why your computer logs into work email at 3 a.m. That's you, answering old colleagues from home.
Your teacher suggests sitting the next-level exam. It's in a month, and you still confuse the words for "pie" and "pier".
At the investor meeting Ingrid introduces you: "Our specialist from abroad." Everyone waits for you to say something exotic.
Karim is training for a marathon on a strict regime and skips lunch all month. You're embarrassed eating a sandwich in front of him. He says it's fine and offers you his coffee.
On video Mom shows you the neighbour's new haircut, the stairwell renovation and how much your nephew's grown. You doze off during the nephew.
Your team switches to hot desking. Every morning you hunt for a free desk, and your mug tours the office separately from you.
Mateo asks you to be the official "family friend" at his son's celebration. You'll need to give a speech.
At the board-game club someone finally explained the rules. You won, and the locals invite you to the next game — Thursday, till midnight.
At your quarterly review Ingrid asks you to rate yourself out of ten. Back home, anything above six was immodest.
The kitchen has a washing-up rota. Your name is misspelled, so for two weeks everyone thought someone else was on duty.
Your sister texts: "Mom's sad, call her more." You call every day. Mom says not for long enough.
Olusegun invites you to morning yoga in the park before work. Starts 6:45 a.m. It's 3°C.
Ingrid asks what you're missing to do your job. Cautiously, you say "nothing", out of habit. Ingrid's disappointed: "Everyone lacks something."
An ex-colleague rings at 11 p.m. asking for a referral to your company. Lovely person, very poor at the job.
The office coffee machine is broken. The locals calmly drink tea. You feel your entire personality runs on coffee.
Yuki invites you to a tea ceremony she's hosting for the team. It lasts two hours and you mustn't speak.
You invite colleagues to dinner for the first time. Two chairs, six guests. Half of them sit on suitcases you never unpacked.
On the tram a tourist asks for directions in your language. For the first time you realise you know this city better than someone.
The "Friday" deadline turns out to be Friday in an office on another continent. So, Saturday morning for you.
There's a festival in the streets tonight, everyone in costume with lanterns. You walk home from work in a business suit and look like part of the show.
Ingrid wants a short update every Friday. You send three pages. She replies: "Too long — three lines, please."
Niko suggests sharing a bigger flat together. He's tidy, fun, and plays the drums at weekends.
You set an alarm for 3 a.m. to wish a friend happy birthday at exactly midnight his time. You've got a presentation in the morning.
Someone accidentally posts a photo of their breakfast in the team chat. Within a minute the whole office has posted theirs. They're waiting for yours.
HR wants your original diploma for verification. It's in Mom's attic next to the New Year decorations, and she's afraid to post it.
right: Ask them to accept a copy

text: The flat's so quiet tonight you put on a radio station from home. It's the weather forecast for your town: rain, plus two.
right: Go sit in a café among people

text: On Thursdays the team breakfasts together, each bringing food in turn. Today is your turn, you learn at 8:50.
A local number calls and talks at length about "your contract". You can't tell if it's the bank, the landlady or a scam.
Mom dictates her pie recipe over video: "Flour by eye, sugar as usual, bake till it's done." You write it down word for word.
A newcomer from another country asks where to get coffee. You proudly show him the coffee machine button it took you three months to learn.
Your project slips because teams in three countries go off for their national holidays back to back. Ingrid wants a one-month plan.
Your first trip home on leave: a night flight with a connection. At 11 p.m. Ingrid sends "one small request" for Monday.
On leave at home, you instinctively greet a neighbour in the language of your new city. The neighbour is alarmed.
Old colleagues take you to lunch while you're home. Everyone asks about life abroad, and you catch yourself boasting about the trams.
The last evening of your leave. Mom is packing a month's worth of food for you. The suitcase won't shut, and you know exactly what overweight costs.
First morning back from leave. Everyone greets you warmly in the local language. Seems you missed them too.
412 emails after your leave. Half are in the local language, and one, judging by the exclamation marks, is very urgent.
You unpack the suitcase from home. The whole flat smells of Mom's kitchen. The neighbours peek in to see what you're cooking.
right: Close the door and savour it

text: Ingrid asks how your leave went, then adds: "Just don't tell me you worked." You did, a little.
In winter the sun rises at nine and sets at three. You arrive and leave in the dark. Ingrid recommends a "sunshine" lamp.
To swap your driving licence you must pass the local exam. The theory is only in the local language, and the "give way" sign is a different shape here.
The team does Secret Santa with a budget and a rule: the gift must say something about your country. You drew Ingrid.
left: Give bread rings and a card

text: You sign up at the gym by your flat. The contract is two pages in the local language, and somewhere it seems to say "three years".
Arjun explains that in his last office everyone said "yes" even when they meant "no". Here people say "no" when they mean "maybe". You're now thoroughly confused.
Your aunt rings to ask whether you've found a partner "over there" yet. The whole family is placing bets. You haven't even found a decent pillow.
Ingrid asks who wants the new project. Here you're expected to volunteer. Back home projects were assigned, and you don't know how to put yourself forward.
The canteen cook remembered you love potatoes and now gives you a double helping every day. You can't refuse now without hurting his feelings.
The annual heating bill arrives. Turns out you've been paying for your neighbour's heating all year: you share a meter.
You've finally learned the local greeting: a slight nod and "good morning". Today you nailed it for the first time. Nobody noticed.
The office on another continent complains to Ingrid that you write "too bluntly". Local colleagues say you're "too soft". You write the same way to both.
Evening: an online course in local history for your residence exam. Question: "What was the first king's name?" You slept through that video.
Annika asks if you'd join the company 10 km run. Sign-up is today; the race is in two months.
A client from your home country wants to deal only with you "because you're one of us". Ingrid's pleased, but now his calls come at night.
Walking by the river this evening, you realise that for the first time you're not thinking about home. Mom rings to ask why you haven't called in ages.
Ngozi notices you're in an hour before everyone again and quietly asks if you're sleeping well. You haven't since the clocks changed.
Ingrid asks you to give new hires an office tour in the local language. You know "kitchen" and "toilet", which may be enough.
A friend from home asks you to translate the manual for a coffee maker she bought abroad. It's in the local language and sixteen pages long.
right: Explain on video in a minute

text: You discover someone broke your cat mug from home and glued it back neatly. There's an apology note on it in three languages.
On a call, someone from another office forgets to mute and loudly discusses your accent with a colleague. Everyone hears, including you.
left: Make a joke in the chat

text: You decide to learn a local dish. The recipe calls for an ingredient sold only on Wednesdays at a market that closes at noon.
Rafael is fifteen minutes late to every meeting and doesn't consider it late. Your client meeting starts in ten minutes, and he's presenting.
HR asks if you'd join the "Culture Ambassador" programme, telling visitors about your country. Payment: chocolate and gratitude.
The landlady drops in unannounced "to check the radiators" and waters your plants while she's at it. Not sure it's legal, but the plants look thrilled.
At the stand-up you openly disagree with Ingrid for the first time. Your voice shakes. Ingrid thanks you and changes the plan.
Samir got the promotion you were also after. He calls you first and suggests celebrating together.
An evening video meeting of residents about whether bikes may be parked in the courtyard. You're elected secretary because you're new.
The new badge fails again this morning. The guard no longer asks and just opens the door: "Morning, foreigner."
You're assigned an intern who arrived from your home country a week ago. He looks at you as a survival expert. You've been here six months.
Sleepless, you walk the city at night. The baker downstairs is already baking and offers you a hot roll for free.
A letter from the tax office in your own language! Delighted, you read it and realise it's machine-translated: "You have been counted, please weep."
At the office party everyone is asked to sing a song in their own language. You can only remember a lullaby and your school anthem.
Your sister sends a video: your cat at Mom's asleep on your jumper. You watch it six times and decide something has to change.
left: Plan to bring the cat over
right: Send the cat a voice note

text: Hana proposes a swap: she teaches you the local language over lunch, you teach her yours. A week later her grasp of yours beats yours of hers.
Ingrid sends edits to your document, all as tracked suggestions in the local language. The "accept all" button looks very tempting.
A friend at home calls in a bad way: break-up, fired, cat unwell. It's 11 p.m. for you, 4 a.m. for him, and he can't sleep.
The immigration office staff recognise you now and say hello. It's your eighth visit. The officer says one more paper is missing.
At team building you must build a raft and cross a lake. Instructions are in the local language. You're in charge of the ropes.
Grandma rings to learn video calls. You started explaining over the phone how to switch the camera on an hour ago.
Lennart says your plan is "not great" and proposes his own. His is better. Everyone looks at you.
The company lawyer warns: spend over a month at home and the tax office may treat you as a non-resident. You planned New Year at Mom's.
The landlady lets you paint the walls "any colour, as long as it isn't bright". You must pick a shade of white from forty options.
Tariq asks you to cover his morning call while he takes his daughter to school. The call is every day at 7:45.
The company rolled out a bot that auto-translates emails. Your "Please, take your time" reached the client as "Please, stop breathing".
right: Switch the bot off for you

text: Someone from the expat chat invites you to a dinner "just like home": dumplings, chat, old songs. You miss it, but tomorrow's your first big client meeting.
Ingrid asks everyone to name one thing they're grateful for this week. You honestly say: "That the laundry room worked."
Ingrid takes you to lunch and pays for everything. Back home you'd insist on paying at least your share. Here, they say, that might offend her.
Your trumpeter neighbour invites you to his concert. You've heard a year of rehearsals through the wall and know the whole programme by heart.
A fire drill at 8:15 a.m. Everyone calmly walks out to the courtyard; you, just in case, carry out your laptop, a folder and your cactus.
The company offers free sessions with a counsellor for foreign staff. Booking goes through Ingrid, and you're shy about writing to her.
Ingrid decides that from Monday all meetings will be in the local language only. "It'll be good for you," she smiles at you personally.
The canteen has a new system: you weigh your food and pay by the gram. You ladled some soup, and it costs as much as a steak.
Mom's first visit: on her very first evening she rearranges all the furniture, rewashes every dish and befriends your neighbour.
Mom asks to see your office. Ingrid unexpectedly agrees and offers her coffee. Mom brings the team homemade pies.
right: Keep it to the café downstairs

text: Mom and Gabriela have been talking through you for two hours. You're translating recipes, gossip and family stories both ways.
Mom's gone home and the flat is quiet again. The fridge holds a month of food, and there's a note on the pillow: "Eat the soup. Call me."
Bruno's leaving the company for another country. As a farewell he gives you his umbrella and says, "You belong here now." You're touched.
right: Hug him and wish him luck

text: You're sent to head office for a week. Another language, other rules, other coffee machines. Back to square one.
The hotel by head office has a night-time alarm. Announcements are in the local language. You're standing outside in pyjamas with colleagues from five countries.
At head office people praise your "cute accent" and ask where it's from. You're not sure anymore: it's a blend of three languages now.
At the head-office meeting everyone speaks very politely and at great length. An hour in, you realise your project was just cancelled.
Returning from head office, you catch yourself thinking: "Home at last." Home being the city you've lived in for eight months.
Annika asks you to mentor a new hire from abroad. You laugh: not long ago you couldn't even buy milk.
You call a local client in the local language for the first time. He replies in English, clearly out of politeness. You stubbornly carry on in the local one.
Your nephew wants "something local". Standing in a souvenir shop, you realise you don't actually know what counts as local here.
For the first time you give a tourist directions in the local language. He thanks you, then asks where your funny accent is from.
The office manager asks you to fill in a "dietary preferences" form for the party. You don't know the names of half the foods listed.
At the party everyone does a local dance and drags you into the circle. You don't know a single step, but they're all waiting.
The train is forty minutes late. Every passenger is owed compensation via an app — in the local language, requiring a local number.
Your mentee messages every half hour: where to buy a SIM, how the shower works, why everyone's silent on the bus. You recognise yourself in him.
Kwame invites you to a film with local subtitles. You read slower than they change and follow the plot from the pictures.
The trumpeter neighbour stops you at the lift: he's off on tour. Would you water his plants and feed his fish?
Two offices want the same report in different formats: slides for one, long text for the other. Ingrid wants everyone happy.
Dad calls to say he's learned to cook your favourite dish and shows it on video. It doesn't look great, but he's very proud.
Leila asks why you apologise when someone steps on your foot. You don't know either — it was just the done thing at home.
At lunch colleagues tell a joke in the local language. For the first time you understand all of it and laugh along. A small victory.
left: Tell a joke of your own

text: You order books in your own language. Shipping costs more than the books, and they'll take two months.
The office coffee machine was replaced with a new one with a different menu. You're back to hot milk. A newcomer from next door is already confidently making cappuccinos.
left: Ask the newcomer to show you

text: Ingrid asks if you see yourself at the company in five years. You don't know if you see yourself in this country in five years.
A newcomer posts in the expat chat: lost his papers, no language, sleeping at the station. He's in your area.
The first snow of the year: five centimetres. The city has ground to a halt and schools are shut, while you, used to snowdrifts, walk to work.
You're the only one in the office: the guard, you and the cactus. Ingrid writes: "Did you actually come in? Go home!"
In the evening you build a snowman in the courtyard, home-style. Neighbours' kids gather to watch, and parents ask where you learned that.
A morning call with an office where it's Friday evening. They're in party mode, chatting about the weekend, while it's Monday for you.
Your intern mixes up local words and says something like "pastry" instead of "thank you" to a client. The client is charmed and asks for the intern on his project.
The neighbours invite you to play a local card game. The rules change with the day of the week and, apparently, the mood.
HR reminds you it's time to renew your residence permit. You'll need a bank letter, a landlady letter and a letter confirming you haven't lost any letters.
left: Gather it all in a week

text: Yuki politely says your laugh in meetings is "very energetic". You can't tell if it's a compliment or a request to laugh quieter.
Your language course offers an evening conversation club with native speakers. First topic: "My perfect weekend".
A six-minute voice note from Mom recorded at 3 a.m. awaits you. It begins: "Don't worry, but…"
Ingrid asks you to present quarterly results on an all-office call. Two hundred listeners, half of them at 11 p.m. their time.
right: Go through it all for an hour

text: There's a street-food festival tonight. For the first time you recognise nearly every dish by name and feel almost local.
right: Grab a favourite and go home

text: Karim asks if you'd cover his weekend on-call shift. In return he'll give you a day of his leave.
The receptionist finally pronounces your name correctly. You're so pleased you want to bring her a cake.
Your sister asks if you regret moving. You think for a long time and realise you don't know.
Your laptop updated overnight and switched the system language to the local one. Now you can't even find the power button.
A local client takes you to lunch and orders "the most traditional thing". It's a cold soup with fish and berries.
On an evening walk you bump into three acquaintances — a colleague, a neighbour and the barista. For the first time here, you don't feel lonely.
Ingrid asks for your opinion first "because you have a fresh perspective". You're not awake yet.
right: Ask for a minute to think

text: The team decides to eat weekly at a restaurant serving one member's home cuisine. This week it's yours. There's only one, and it's awful.
left: Take them to the awful one

text: In the lift the company CEO asks your name and how you like the city. Four floors to go. You know just two answers in the local language.
The CEO sits at your canteen table with a tray like any employee. Everyone else keeps eating. You forget how to hold a fork.
At 3 a.m. the smoke alarm starts chirping every forty seconds: low battery. It's on a high ceiling and you have no ladder.
left: Knock next door for a ladder

text: In the new office Wednesday is meeting-free. Your old team back home books calls with you on Wednesdays precisely because "you're free then".
The office posts a spreadsheet of everyone's salaries — normal here. You see you earn less than a colleague who joined in the same role a month after you.
Ingrid announces the whole office closes for three weeks in July. Leave is mandatory. You'd been saving days for a winter trip home.
The company introduces time tracking: every half hour you log what you're doing in a system in the local language. There's no option for "trying to understand the system".
A local recruiter calls with an offer: higher pay, closer office. But your work permit is tied to your current company.
You must choose a pension fund from forty options. The descriptions are in the local language and all promise "stability and growth".
First visit to a local barber. You try to explain "just a little shorter". The barber nods knowingly and picks up the clippers.
You come to work after the barber with a very short haircut. Ingrid says: "Bold!" You're not sure it's a compliment.
You wake up to 214 new messages in the family chat. While you slept, they argued, made up and decided who's visiting Grandma.
You need to book a repairman by phone. Talking on the phone in the local language is scarier than presenting to the board.
It's bring-your-child-to-work day. Ngozi's daughter sits next to you and corrects your grammar every minute.
An ex-colleague sees your social post captioned in the local language and writes: "So you only talk like that now?"
HR wants a short intro video for the intranet, answering "What surprised you about our country?" without offending anyone.
Ingrid asks why you always agree to everything other offices ask. "You're allowed to say no," she reminds you.
You go to a local cooking class with colleagues. The chef talks fast, and you add to the dough what everyone else adds to the sauce.
The company bans paper cups: everyone must bring their own mug. Your favourite cat mug is being repaired at Gabriela's.
right: Buy a mug from the machine

text: The staff newsletter wants to interview you for "Our Internationals". First question: "What do you miss most?"
For a week the neighbour's cat has been coming to dine through your open window. You're attached, and the neighbour's getting suspicious.
You're sending money to your parents. The bank charges a fee, the rate is poor and the transfer takes five days. Mom's already at the shop.
Mateo suggests you both jump ship: "They pay more and lunch is free." Your visa is tied to this company.
At 9 p.m. a client from home rings, surprised you've "gone to bed so early". It's 9 p.m., you're in pyjamas, but awake.
In the morning, all that's left of your bike outside is the wheel locked to the post. Great wheel, excellent lock.
You report the bike theft. The officer fills in a form, asking twenty questions about its colour, make and personality.
It's Grandma's big birthday. The family's at the table, and you're on a laptop between the salads. They keep forgetting to turn you towards whoever's talking.
right: Ask someone to hold the camera

text: The internet technician will come "between 8 and 6". You took the day off; at 5:55 p.m. he rings to say he'll come tomorrow.
right: Ask the neighbour to let him in

text: On the intranet everyone lists hobbies: sailing, mountains, pottery. Yours is "learning the language and not getting lost".
Sunday night. The city's gone quiet, the shops are shut, and you're so homesick you want to buy a ticket right now.
The office introduces a clear-desk policy: everything goes into lockers at night. Your locker came with a code nobody remembers.
right: Carry it all in your backpack

text: At a feedback workshop you're asked to tell a colleague to their face what you dislike about their work. The colleague is Ingrid.
First visit to the gym you signed up for. The trainer explains exercises in the local language, and you do everything half a second late.
right: Work out to videos at home

text: In the morning colleagues congratulate you on a holiday you've never heard of. Apparently it's your country's day by the local calendar.
Ingrid asks you to write a short "About our team" blurb for the website. You write three paragraphs; marketing cuts it to "We".
The courier left your parcel with a neighbour you've never seen. His door has a sign: "Do not disturb until 2026."
The driving instructor speaks only the local language, very calmly. You understand "stop" just after you've driven past.
On a five-country call someone asks, "What time is it for everyone?" The next fifteen minutes go on time zones.
right: Joke and get back on track

text: Your best friend back home has also been offered a job abroad and asks your advice. For a long while you don't know what to say.
Your brother asks you to get him into your company. Lovely person, but he speaks neither English nor the local language.
Every canteen dish has fifteen allergen icons. You spend fifteen minutes studying the key, and lunch goes cold.
Your cousin's getting married. You watch the ceremony on video at 6 a.m. in pyjamas, crying along with your aunt.
Elsa says the office sauna runs on Fridays and the whole team goes, Ingrid included. Sometimes meetings happen there too.
The company sends you to a first-aid course in the local language. You practise bandaging a colleague, three seconds behind the instructions.
right: Ask for the handouts in advance

text: You've been made floor fire warden. You must learn the rules in the local language and run a drill monthly.
Your company card is declined at the café where you're lunching with a client. He's waiting. Your personal card is only half-local too.
You fix your bike yourself with a video in the local language. Just a mechanic's hands and baffling subtitles. Three parts are left over.
Mom rings at 6 a.m. your time "to catch you before work". You asked for nothing before eight, but she mixed up the time zones.
right: Gently remind her of the time

text: You're running a project across three continents. Each night you write an update that's read while you sleep and answered while you're still asleep.
At dinner, Ingrid's family speak only the local language. You get about sixty percent and nod through the rest.
This morning the building chat shows a photo of your rubbish bag by the wrong bin, captioned "One of the newcomers?" You're the only newcomer.
Ingrid tells you your probation is extended by a month: "Nothing serious, we just want to get to know you better." It sounds serious.
Grandma calls and mistakes you for her neighbour. She talks seedlings for five minutes before realising you're abroad.
At 6:40 a.m. you're on a train to a meeting in another city. The whole carriage sleeps; only you rehearse your talk in a whisper in the local language.
A client from yet another country writes in a mix of English and their language. You reply in a mix of English and yours. You seem to have agreed on something.
You bought a sun lamp against the winter blues. Switched it on, and the neighbours opposite drew their curtains. Seems it's rather bright.
The bus driver doesn't take cash. You haven't got your card, and the meeting is in twenty minutes. A passenger behind offers to pay for you.
Niko asks to swap leave slots: he wants your July, you'd get November. In November it's dark here by four.
The neighbours invite you for dinner and serve a dish you eat with your hands. You're used to forks and fear doing it wrong.
Oscar returns your expense report for the fourth time. Now the problem is the receipt's "too crumpled to scan".
Mandatory online security training: four hours, local language only, followed by a forty-question test.
You find a series from home and binge three episodes. By the fourth you realise you miss the local one with the grandma.
left: Go back to the local show

text: You've started morning runs like the locals. On day three a pensioner with a dog overtakes you and cheers you on in the local language.
Ngozi is back from parental leave and doesn't recognise half the processes. She asks you, "as an ex-newbie", to help her settle back in.
An internet bill arrives, though you were never connected. Support is a robot in the local language, and it's very polite.
A newcomer from your home country joins the team. Everyone expects you to become best friends. You have nothing in common except the language.
Head office wants a video from you for staff worldwide: "Why I love our company". You get ten minutes to film it.
At midnight an email from another office: "Are you awake? Got a minute?" It's noon for them, and it's all urgent.
Your barista is off on holiday and introduces his stand-in: "This is our regular, the usual." The stand-in has no idea what "the usual" is.
Ingrid asks why you never take sick days. Here they believe ill employees infect everyone and sap morale.
In the evening you look out at the building opposite. In every window someone's dining, reading, laughing. You wave at the woman across; she waves back.
On the morning train the inspector checks IDs. Your residence card is a new design he's never seen. He calls a colleague over.
Samir asks you to translate a card for his mother-in-law into your language. She's from your home country, and Samir wants to impress.
A classmate invites you to an online reunion. Everyone talks kids, mortgages and summer houses. They ask you: "So how are you, is it OK there?"
You try to bring your bike on the metro at rush hour. The locals look horrified: it's only allowed after nine.
Ingrid offers everyone an hour of yoga in work time once a week. You're shy, but skipping it would make you stand out.
A friend from home is coming on holiday and wants to stay ten days. You have one room and a trumpeter neighbour.
In the morning your friend wants a city tour, but it's a workday. He's sure that abroad everyone works "whenever they like".
right: Give him a route and go

text: Your friend pops into the office "for a minute", loudly marvelling at how lovely it all is. Colleagues smile politely. Ingrid offers him coffee.
Your friend leaves, and for the first time you see your city through his eyes. It turns out you've come to love a lot here.
Ingrid holds a meeting on the way to the café. You take notes on your phone, trip and step in a puddle.
right: Ask to finish in the office

text: Sales want you to call a client from your country and talk him into a smaller discount, "one compatriot to another".
In the evening you realise you missed bulky-waste day. The old mattress will sit in your hallway for another month.
