Ingrid asks you to meet a delegation at the airport with a sign. You write their surnames and aren't sure how they're pronounced.
The delegation is from your home country, and you're told to be "interpreter, guide and friend". Ingrid's report is still due.
The delegation wants "something homey" tonight. You take them to the city's only restaurant serving your cuisine. It's closed for renovation.
The morning after the delegation you've lost your voice: three days of interpreting, joking and singing. You present to the team at 10.
The delegation sent Ingrid a thank-you letter naming you personally. Ingrid forwards it to the whole office: "So proud!"
In the evening the wind turns your umbrella inside out and carries it off. You stand in the rain; passers-by nod sympathetically — they've no umbrellas either.
A fine arrives in the morning: you cycled without a light two weeks ago. Cameras here notice even bikes.
Jorge asks you to attend his internal talk and ask a planted question "to warm up the room".
In the evening you notice you're thinking in a mix of three languages. You can only remember the word for "fridge" in the local one.
Ingrid asks everyone for one word describing their mood. You say a word in the local language. It turns out to mean "dumpling".
Two offices argue in a shared chat over whose report format is better. Both ask you to back them, as the "neutral party".
At night you read the news from home and can't sleep. You have an important meeting in the morning, but your head is 3,000 km away.
On your desk: a bag from Gabriela with a scarf she knitted and a note, "For your first winter here." You don't know what to give back.
In a quality review you spot an error in Ingrid's report. Small, but it's in the board presentation.
You join the library. The librarian suggests children's books "to start" and hands you a book about a duckling.
Ingrid is ten minutes late to a meeting for the first time. Everyone looks at you, the new "punctuality expert".
Ingrid tells you you've passed probation. You're so pleased you hug her. Here, it seems, people don't hug the boss.
HR informs you that unused leave expires here in March. You have nineteen days, and March is the project launch.
Priya asks you to cover: she's leaving early for a parents' evening. If Ingrid asks, she's "meeting a client".
The phone bill arrives: you forgot calls home aren't included in the Sparrow plan. It's a week's groceries.
Immigration does random address checks and turns up at 7:30 a.m. You open the door in pyjamas holding a toothbrush.
right: Ask them to come back later

text: Everyone leaves for lunch in groups while you linger at your desk. By the time you go, the canteen is half empty and you lunch with the security guard.
In a shop window tonight you catch your reflection: local raincoat, local bike, local bread under your arm. You barely recognise yourself.
You're working from home, and at 9 a.m. the neighbours start drilling. At 9:30 you present to head office.
Olusegun says you've gone too local: silent in the lift, no greetings on the bus. He's joking, but it makes you a little sad.
At 2 a.m. your brother calls: he forgot the time difference and wants to show off his new guitar. He can't really play yet.
right: Ask him to send a video

text: A client meeting at 8 a.m. in a café. You arrive at 7:55 to find the client got there at 7:45 and has already finished his coffee.
New kitchen rules are posted: coffee only from your own mug, no touching others'. Your mug is still at Gabriela's.
You're offered a flat overlooking the river. Pricier, further from work, but with a balcony where drying laundry is allowed.
Moving morning. The movers speak a local dialect you can't follow and load your sofa into the wrong van.
After the move you must update your address in six places: bank, tax office, immigration, insurer, work and library.
left: Do it all in one day

text: The new neighbours bring a pie and a note. You understand the note fully without a translator and nearly cry with pride.
The new route to work takes ten minutes longer but goes through the park. For the first time in a year you're not rushing.
Ingrid asks you to speak at a conference in your home country on the company's behalf. Your ex-boss will be in the audience.
You're home for two days for the conference. Mom wants you to sleep at hers; the venue is across town.
At the conference your ex-boss comes up: "I always knew you'd go far. Literally." He offers you a senior role back home.
You present in your own language after a year of the local one. You mix up words and twice say "thank you" in the local language. The room laughs kindly.
Friends gather for you at your old favourite café. An hour in, you catch yourself waiting for the bill so everyone can pay their own share.
At the airport you realise you're flying "home" — to another country. Mom cries at the check-in desk.
Back at the office, Ingrid asks if you'll consider your ex-boss's offer. Someone has already told her.
Tonight you sit with two offers: stay here or go home. The cat you finally brought over is asleep on both printouts.
The cat you finally brought over has spent three days under the bath, emerging only at night. You're late from coaxing him to eat.
Tariq asks you to help him move to another town on Saturday. He has pizza and six wardrobes.
Dad sends a voice message: "Mom and I have thought about it: live wherever you're happy." You listen three times.
In the morning you tell your ex-boss you're staying. He replies: "I thought so." You feel lighter.
Ingrid hears you're staying and suggests discussing a promotion. But it requires passing the next-level local language exam.
right: Ask for it without the exam

text: You study every evening. Your neighbour Gabriela offers to help and speaks only the local language to you, even when you're in tears.
right: Ask for some English now and then

text: Exam morning. Task one: write a noise complaint to a neighbour. You have extensive practical experience.
In the oral exam you're asked what you think of the local weather. You speak for two minutes without complaining once.
Results arrive tonight: you passed, with a "satisfactory". Your local colleagues congratulate you as if you'd won the Olympics.
Mateo jokingly calls you "practically local" and teaches you a new five-move handshake.
You're promoted to lead a small team: three people from three countries, one of them your former intern.
In the evening you write your first email to your new team. You redraft it nine times to make it direct, gentle and warm all at once.
right: Say it all in a meeting

text: Your team's first stand-up. You start at 9:00 sharp, as is done here. Your ex-intern arrives at 9:03, embarrassed and apologetic.
You must give a team member direct feedback, local-style. You rehearse in the mirror but keep softening it the way you would at home.
Mom heard about the promotion and told the neighbours, your aunt and your old teacher. Now they all ask when you'll be "a big boss".
You get a team budget. Each person wants something different: language classes, a conference trip, a new coffee machine.
Two of your team, from different countries, can't agree on meeting style: one wants to discuss everything, the other to decide at once.
You wake at night convinced you forgot to send the head-office report. You check — you sent it. But now you can't sleep.
A newcomer from abroad joins your team. On day one he can't get through the turnstile, and you see yourself in him.
You write a forty-item checklist for the newcomer. Item one: "Don't panic." You smile: the circle is complete.
You put together a "survival kit" for the newcomer: adapter, umbrella, bike map and a chocolate bar. You needed all this a year ago.
You're invited to your first leaders' meeting. Everyone's on gym balls. You sit confidently and don't even roll towards the window.
Head office wants you to write an article on adapting to a new country. You can choose the title, but every office in the world will read it.
It's exactly a year since you landed. You find the first photo on your phone: the suitcase, the cat on it and a note: "Don't panic."
Colleagues give you a cake in the morning. Your name's spelled right, and the little flag is — this time — the correct country.
Ingrid asks you to sum up your year in three words. After a long think you say: "Scary, funny, mine."
The fog's so thick this morning you walk straight past your office and end up at a bakery on the far side of the block.
You write a client a word that means "my sympathies" in your language but sounds nearly like "congratulations" in the local one. He's just lost a big order.
The shared laundry now takes payment by app. The app rejects your card. Your slot ends at 10 p.m. and the washing's already in the drum.
HR asks why your timesheet shows local holidays but not your home country's. You're entitled to those too.
On a call, a colleague from another office has an accent so thick you catch every other word. He seems to have the same trouble with you.
Your first dinner on the new balcony. The upstairs neighbour lowers a basket of apples on a rope with a note: "Welcome."
It snowed and your bike's buried. Local colleagues have already fitted studded winter tyres. You haven't.
Sun-mi proposes a team "home cooking day" and asks you to make something from your country. Everyone else has promised three dishes.
The building manager writes: roof repairs from 7 a.m. tomorrow. You're working from home with a 7:30 call.
left: Head to the office by seven
right: Take the call from a café

text: Ingrid asks why you send emails at 11 p.m. "I don't want the team thinking it's expected." Those were emails to your mother.
The new canteen cook makes something very like a dish from your childhood. You close your eyes and for a minute you're home.
Your nephew wants to learn local swear words to impress classmates. Your sister is waving her arms off-screen.
right: Refuse in front of your sister

text: An interpreter works the partner meeting. Your local language is good enough now to notice he's translating inaccurately.
Karim asks how people in your country congratulate a new baby — he wants to send your sister a message. You're touched.
At 10:05 p.m. the downstairs neighbour knocks: you dropped a pot. Your apology in the local language is so good he stays to chat for half an hour.
This morning someone locked their bike to yours. No owner in sight, and your meeting is in fifteen minutes.
The annual staff survey asks: "Do you feel part of the team?" Scale of 1–10. A year ago you'd have said 2.
You order dinner via an app at 9 p.m. The courier calls, speaking fast in dialect, and all you get is that he's at some other door.
Every morning you start by checking the time in six cities. It takes longer than breakfast.
left: Hang six clocks on the wall

text: A local client asks for an impossible deadline. You've learned to say no the local way — short, no apologies. Your heart still pounds.
You switch on local radio and understand the host's joke for the first time. You laugh so loudly alone in the kitchen that the cat leaves the room.
The office on another continent switches to summer time; yours doesn't. Every call shifts by an hour, and you find out by joining an empty one.
Elsa tells you her family also emigrated when she was a child. She still sometimes dreams in her grandmother's language.
You decide to order pizza by phone, in the local language, no app. Order accepted. An hour later, sushi arrives.
right: Call back and sort it out

text: A 7 a.m. call with another continent. You're jolted awake by everyone saying your name. Apparently you were asked something.
IT has finally labelled the coffee machine in three languages, yours included. In your language, "cappuccino" became "cat's milk".
Your aunt asks what you're eating and demands a fridge photo. It's packed with local food, and she doesn't recognise a single item.
You've finally put your name on the mailbox. For the first time in a year, the postman leaves your post instead of taking it back.
At the party Ingrid asks everyone for their funniest mistake of the year. You don't know which of your two hundred to choose.
left: Tell the "I am a potato" one

text: Everything went wrong: you misunderstood a client, mixed up times and got soaked. Tonight in a café you want to go home — really home.
After the bad day Kwame sends a photo: your first day a year ago, looking lost at the turnstile. Caption: "Look how far you've come."
right: Save it and get to work

text: Colleagues talk holiday plans: a lake cabin, a boat, no internet. Ingrid suggests you come along.
First evening at the lake cabin. No internet, and Mom doesn't know you're alive. Colleagues are grilling fish and singing.
left: Drive to the village for signal

text: Ingrid wakes you at 5 a.m. to go fishing. It's a local tradition and refusing is rude, they say. You've never held a rod.
You catch the only fish of the day. Everyone cheers, but the fish looks so sad you want to set it free.
Your last evening at the lake. Colleagues ask you to sing a song in your language. You do, and someone hums along without the words.
Back in town in the morning. Your phone finds signal: 86 messages — 40 from Mom, 46 from work.
After the holiday you feel you've forgotten the local language. Your first sentence in the meeting takes two minutes to build.
Kwame suggests visiting your country together next year: "You can show me where buckwheat grows."
A newcomer asks how you dealt with homesickness. You think and realise there's no answer — you've just learned to live with it.
The bank credits your salary twice by mistake. Locals say the bank will notice on its own. But you remember how hard it was to open that account.
Your cat has learned to use the shared balcony and now dines with every neighbour in turn. One sends you a photo: "Yours is at ours."
You arrive Monday to an empty office. Not a holiday — everyone's working from home, and you skimmed past the notice in the local language.
Mid-presentation to five countries, your internet drops. You carry on via your phone, holding it above the laptop.
It rains all weekend. The locals stroll in it happily. You watch from the window, wondering whether to finally go native.
Your cat has stuck to your home-town time zone and wakes you at 4 a.m. demanding breakfast.
A local client praises your work and adds: "You're not like a foreigner at all." You're not sure if that's a compliment.
Mom sends a knitted jumper with an enormous reindeer. Tomorrow is ugly-jumper day at the office. Perfect timing.
You wear Mom's reindeer jumper and win the contest. The prize is an extra day off. Mom demands a photo with the trophy.
right: Give the day off to a colleague

text: In the company's global chat someone asks how to say "good luck" in every language. You post yours, and within a minute someone makes it their status.
At 8 a.m. Ingrid wants a contract translated into your language by lunch. You don't know the legal terms even in your own language.
Rafael tells a joke about your country loudly in the canteen. It's funny, but you've heard it twelve times from different people.
Your old landlady won't return the deposit: "a stain on the carpet". It was there before you, and you have a photo — on a broken phone.
left: Repair the phone for the photo

text: You miss your morning train to a business trip: the platform change was announced in the local language. You were on the old one.
You realise the colleagues chatting at the coffee machine in the local language are discussing you. They think you still can't understand.
You've booked flights home for the holidays, but head office schedules an audit for exactly those dates. Ingrid apologises but asks you to stay.
The head-office auditor asks questions in a third language you don't know. The interpreter is stuck in traffic.
The auditor finds an error in your report: you converted currency at last year's rate. The amount is small, but Ingrid goes pale.
In the evening your family sends a photo of the festive table without you. Mom set your plate "just in case". You're at the office with the auditor.
right: Put the phone away and work

text: Mom calls in the morning: Grandma's unwell. Nothing serious, but you want to be there. Flights are expensive and your leave isn't approved.
Ingrid hears about your grandma and offers you a week off herself. "Work can wait." You fear it won't wait very well.
Grandma has recovered and sternly asks why you flew in when "there's so much to do at work". She's proud and scolding at once.
A neighbour files a complaint with the building manager: your cat "disturbs the peace" at night. As far as you know, the cat sleeps.
right: Reply to the complaint in writing

text: The other office's team blew their part of the project, but you're answerable to Ingrid. Their manager isn't replying: it's their national holiday.
The night before the project's due. Third coffee in, you realise the local language has no word for your state. Yours has several.
right: Bed at two, up at six

text: You deliver the project in the morning. Ingrid says "good" without "very". You've spent a year learning that's top praise, and you're still disappointed.
You accidentally send an email meant for Mom to the company-wide mailing list. It's in your language and opens: "Mum, everyone here is weird."
That evening it turns out the translation bot rendered your email to Mom for anyone curious. Five colleagues write: "We're weird too, don't worry."
right: Hide in your office for a week

text: The cat smashed the pot of the plant Gabriela left with you while she's away. The plant survived; the pot, her grandmother's, didn't.
In a meeting, a colleague from another office sharply criticises your team in front of everyone. Normal by local standards; by yours, a scandal.
A friend from home rings to say you've "changed" and become "kind of cold". You've just started writing shorter messages.
The office lift is broken; a sign in the local language promises a fix "shortly". Your team's on the ninth floor and you're holding boxes of documents.
Your former intern made an error, but the client blames you as team lead. The intern begs you not to tell Ingrid it was him.
The bathroom bulb blows in the evening. At the shop you face a wall of thirty bulb types with baffling fittings.
right: Bring the old one and ask

text: A summons arrives in the morning, in the local language. You panic for ten minutes before realising it's an invitation to a residents' meeting.
Ingrid's on holiday and left you in charge. On day one head office calls with a question only she can answer.
In the evening you reread your decision and doubt every word. Lennart texts: "You did it right." You don't believe him.
With Ingrid away, everyone's relaxed and drifting in at ten. You've absorbed the local punctuality and are now the strictest person on the team.
Hana tells you she's leaving: going back to her home country. "It's nice here, but my mum's there." You understand all too well.
At Hana's farewell everyone toasts in their own language. You speak in the local one, and Hana cries. So do you.
Hana's desk is empty this morning, with a note for you: "Don't forget your lunchtime walk." Ingrid asks who'll take Hana's projects.
You're doing Hana's projects plus your own. You've skipped lunch three days running, though her note is right in front of you.
Hana texts from home: "Mum says hi. Are you eating lunch?" You're at the office at 9 p.m. with a sandwich.
You take down the clock showing your home-town time. Now there's only local time on the wall, and you feel a little guilty.
The bank calls: your account is frozen for review after a transfer from Mom labelled "for pies". The system found it suspicious.
Your account's frozen and payday is a week off. You've a little cash, which hardly anywhere here accepts.
The bank unfreezes your account in the morning and sends an apology in the local language. You understand every word and are prouder of that than of the money.
In a meeting Samir passes off your idea as his own. Ingrid praises Samir. You sit beside him in silence.
left: Speak up in front of all

text: In the evening you catch yourself checking the work chat every five minutes. Nothing's happening, but you can't stop.
The meeting you prepped all night for is cancelled five minutes before the start, no reason given. The calendar just says "postponed".
The canteen heating is off and everyone eats in coats. The cook cheerfully says cold soup is traditional. Today's soup is cold too.
At 11:30 p.m. a colleague in another office writes: "Not urgent, but please reply now." You're already in bed.
A city marathon closes every road this morning. You find out on a bus that hasn't moved in forty minutes.
Head office books you a trip departing Saturday morning "so no workdays are lost". You promised to help Kwame move.
On the trip you're put in a windowless hotel room. You lose track of day and night and ring Mom at 3 a.m. her time.
right: Ask for a room with a window

text: At the hotel breakfast the waiter speaks the fourth language of your life. You silently point at an egg and coffee.
At the talks, the partners confer in their own language, assuming you can't follow. You can — it's close to the local one.
You get back to your flat late at night. The cat's sulking, the plants have wilted and the neighbour left a note: "We fed him. All fine."
Ingrid calls you in and says she can see you're tired. "You're doing two people's work. I'll hire help, but you'll have to train them."
You interview a candidate from abroad. He's as nervous as you were a year ago, mixing up local words.
Your new assistant arrives twenty minutes before you on day one and has already rearranged your desk "systematically".
Explaining a task to your assistant in the local language, you confuse "urgent" and "never". He diligently doesn't do it.
The neighbours throw a courtyard party ending at exactly 10 p.m. You're invited, but you have a 7 a.m. call with another continent.
Morning: two team members are arguing about deadlines in the chat. One writes in caps; the other in a language you don't know.
right: Wait for them to cool off

text: You take your team to lunch on the budget for the first time. Everyone orders their home cuisine, and the bill is triple the limit.
On Friday evening head office wants a report by Monday. You'd promised yourself a work-free weekend, the first in a month.
The tax office asks why you paid tax in two countries at once. You'd like to know that yourself.
Ngozi asks you to sign a group letter to Ingrid about workloads. You agree with it but fear for your visa.
Mom asks why you go to bed so late. You honestly mention work, and she lectures you on health for half an hour.
The radiators are off: the heating runs on a schedule, and the schedule says it's still summer. It's 6°C outside.
On a call, someone from a far-off office asks you to slow down. You do, and everyone else starts nodding off.
The shop selling food from home is closing. The owner is clearing stock at a discount and sadly says "compatriots don't buy enough".
Mom calls at 6 a.m.: her tap's broken and she wants you to talk her through it on video. You're not a plumber in any language.
At your half-year review Ingrid says you're "too cautious". Back home you were praised for that. Here it costs you bonus points.
In the evening you make two lists: what's better here and what's better at home. They come out the same length, which scares you.
At 8 a.m. the landlady arrives with a repairman: "We warned you by letter." The letter came last night in the local language.
left: Let them in and be late
right: Leave them a key and go

text: Olusegun asks if you'd do a party sketch with him: "How I Learned the Local Language". He's already written the script.
Evening rehearsal with Olusegun. In the script you play the turnstile. It's the most honest role of your life.
The morning after the party everyone's quoting your turnstile sketch. The CEO says in the lift: "Beep-beep! Access denied!"
After the turnstile sketch you're asked to perform at every event. You've become "that funny foreigner" when you wanted to be known as good at your job.
The phone rings at night: an unknown number from home. A school friend you haven't heard from in ten years. He's moved abroad too and wants advice.
Dad wants to visit, but his visa needs your invitation certified in three places. One of them opens two hours a week.
Dad's here and wants to see "how you work". Ingrid allows it, so Dad spends the day in a corner of the office with a newspaper from home.
By evening Dad, without a word of the local language, has befriended every neighbour. He's playing cards with them and seems to be winning.
At the airport Dad says: "I'm at peace now. You've got good people here." You stand at check-in unable to say a word.
You get to the office an hour late from the airport. Ingrid says nothing, but your calendar now has a meeting titled "Shall we talk?"
The flat is quiet again tonight. Dad's cup is on the table. The cat sleeps on the jumper Dad "accidentally" left behind.
The company organises a volunteer park clean-up. 8 a.m. Saturday. Ingrid's already holding a rake.
The CEO mentions your team in a company-wide email. Your three-person team is jubilant. The next department looks sideways.
A colleague from the next department writes in chat: "Foreigners always get more attention." Not to you, but you see it.
You end up in the lift with that same colleague. He greets you awkwardly. Six floors of silence.
Ingrid pairs you with that colleague on a new project. He suggests a "clean slate" and offers you a coffee.
left: Accept the coffee and the truce

text: The last bus left at 11 p.m., two minutes early. The locals are outraged, as if it's a national disaster. You just start walking.
Your carrier texts: the Sparrow plan is ending and you're being moved to Penguin. Not even the carrier knows what Penguin includes.
Zeynep asks you to be her "cultural interpreter" in a meeting with a client from your country. You'll be translating pauses, not words.
Mom sends you the winter coat you wore at school. She's convinced it still fits.
left: Wear it and send a photo

text: Your team signs up for the corporate run. As lead you're expected to set the pace, and the last time you ran was for a bus.
In a meeting with a client from your country you're asked to interpret. For the first time you translate local into native and muddle both.
In the evening you realise your closest friends now live in three different countries and you chat in a blend of four languages.
Ingrid runs a mandatory safety-rules quiz. You score 100%. Local colleagues get 70% and are stunned.
Lennart accidentally sent a client your draft with comments in your language. The client is from your country and understood everything.
In the evening you practise tomorrow's apology to the client in the mirror, in three languages. The cat watches disapprovingly.
In the morning the client from your country calls, laughing: "Your comments were the best thing I've read all year. Let's keep working." You exhale.
You're invited to present to the board. Everyone there wears suits; your office lives in jumpers. You don't know what to wear.
Your brother admits he envies your "life abroad". You tell him about cold soup, turnstiles and eight trips to immigration.
You've bought studded tyres like the locals and cycle on snow for the first time. A pensioner with a rack full of fir trees overtakes you.
Your team has its own tradition: on Fridays each person teaches everyone one word in their language. It's your turn.
For the first time in ages, a weekend with no plans. You wake at seven out of habit and don't know what to do with yourself.
Over morning coffee Ingrid admits she too once moved from another country. "For two years I cried in the lift." You laugh — it's practically a tradition.
The company offers an exchange: three months in an office on another continent. A new language again, a new flat, a new turnstile.
This morning the street outside is closed and the pavement torn up. To leave, you must cross a plank over a hole. The workers wave politely.
You spend an hour chatting with the insurer's bot in the local language. Finally it offers to "speak to a human" — during business hours, which have just ended.
Your ex-colleague Sveta rings: "Everything's fallen apart without you. Kidding. But come and visit." You laugh and feel a little wistful.
In the morning HR sends the visa renewal form. Same questions as a year ago, but now you understand them without a translator.
Niko suggests you go in on a four-person boat with colleagues. Everyone here does it. You can't swim.
You sign up for swimming lessons. The coach gives instructions in the local language, and you mix up "breathe in" and "breathe out".
right: Learn from videos in your language

text: Saturday morning, they're waiting at the boat. You turn up in a life jacket over your coat. Colleagues are thrilled and take photos.
Immigration changes the rules: renewal now needs a language certificate. Yours is one level short.
In the evening you open the next-level textbook. Topic one: "Expressing doubt politely." You feel like a pro.
right: Bask in it and close the book

text: Your sister rings in the morning: she wants to move abroad too. Mom's in shock and blames it all on you.
Ingrid asks you to run a workshop for other managers: "Working with an International Team". The CEO is in the group.
Preparing slides tonight, you add the photo of the turnstile from your first day. You wonder if it's too personal.
At your workshop the CEO laughs loudest at the "I am a potato" story and asks for it to be part of new-hire onboarding.
A newcomer from next door is crying in the meeting room. You recognise the lift syndrome and knock. He says even the coffee machine doesn't understand him.
You decide to start a club for foreign newcomers at work. First meeting at your place. Twelve people turn up, plus a cat.
Ingrid hears about your club and wants to make it an official company programme. With reports, a budget and targets.
For the first time you book a holiday somewhere other than home: the seaside in a neighbouring country. Mom's hurt: "And when are you visiting us?"
Packing for the sea, you find a note at the bottom from your first move: "Don't forget the jam." You never did get that jam here.
On the beach in the morning you hear four languages and understand three. A year ago it was one.
On the beach an email from head office arrives, flagged "urgent". You hold your phone over the water and think.
At a seaside café the waiter asks where you're from. For the first time you answer with the name of your new city.
Back from holiday, your cat ignores you for three days. The neighbour says he missed you and sang at night.
Mateo has become a citizen and invites you to the ceremony, where you'll need to sing the anthem. You only know the tune.
After the ceremony you wonder for the first time whether you'll ever want citizenship here. No answer, just insomnia.
There's a flower from your team on your desk this morning, with a note in three languages: "Thanks for being with us." You don't know the occasion.
Turns out it's the local "mentor day", and your team picked you. Ingrid laughs: "A year ago you couldn't find the loo."
In the evening Mom says Dad's been feeling unwell but "didn't want to worry you". You're hearing this a week late.
In the morning you ask Ingrid for a week of unpaid leave. She asks no questions, only whether you need help with tickets.
Dad's nearly well and grumbles that you shouldn't have come. But he holds your hand all evening. The work chat is exploding.
Sitting in Mom's kitchen tonight, you realise you miss your flat over there. And over there, you miss this kitchen.
At the airport Dad hands you a jar of pickles "for your colleagues". Customs, as you know, loves pickles.
You bring Dad's pickles to the office. Within an hour the jar's empty, and Olusegun wants the recipe for his mum.
After a week at home you've 300 emails and three missed deadlines. The team coped without you, and somehow that stings a little.
In the morning you learn the team made a big decision while you were away. It's a good decision.
right: Ask to be consulted next time

text: Dad rings in the afternoon to say he went for his first walk today. You're in a meeting but step into the corridor.
You decide to call your parents daily at the same time. The only slot that suits everyone is your lunch break.
You're lunching with your parents on video in the canteen. Colleagues sit down and wave at Mom. She's thrilled and demands introductions.
In the evening you can't remember the word "fork" in any language. You stand over the cutlery drawer feeling your brain is full.
You notice your new visa has your name wrong: one extra letter. Your business trip is in a week.
At the border the officer stares at the extra letter in your name for ages. Behind you queues your company's delegation.
Your flight's cancelled and you spend the night at the airport with colleagues. Lennart pulls a board game from his backpack. You've never seen him without a tie.
You land for the meeting with no sleep. The client suggests starting "with a short tour of the plant". On foot. Three hours.
right: Ask to get straight to business

text: In the negotiations you start answering in your city's language, not the client's. He smiles politely.
On the train home tonight you realise you call the city you've lived in for a year "home". Mom would be hurt.
Your team decides to start each morning with "How are you, really?" Answering "fine" is banned.
A client wants an "off the books" discount so his boss won't know. That's not done here. Back home, it happened.
An ordinary Tuesday. You're cooking, talking to Mom and to the neighbour across the balcony in two languages. Suddenly you realise you're happy.
The office turnstile's broken this morning and won't let anyone in. The guard looks at you: "You know what to do with it." You really do.
left: Fix it with your trademark thump
right: Wait for the repairman with everyone

text: Ingrid announces she's moving to an office on another continent in a month. She offers you her job.
In the evening you weigh Ingrid's offer. More responsibility, more calls at odd hours, less time for Mom.
right: Decline and stay with the team

text: Ingrid gives away her plants in the morning. You get a cactus and a note: "Water monthly. Don't overwork — daily."
left: Pin the note above your desk

text: Ingrid's replacement comes from head office. He speaks a third language, loves long meetings and hugs hello.
In the evening the new manager messages you: "Why is everyone silent in meetings? Don't they like me?" You see yourself a year ago.
The new manager's first meeting runs two hours instead of fifteen minutes. The team looks at you imploringly.
The new manager hugs everyone at stand-up. Local colleagues turn to stone. He heads for you as his "fellow foreigner".
left: Hug him and save the moment

text: You now explain local customs to the boss and his habits to the locals. It's not in your job description, but it eats half your day.
left: Ask for it to be in your job spec
right: Keep doing it as a favour

text: The boss asks why lunches here are so short. "Where I'm from, lunch is two hours and conversation." The locals look at you.
right: Say it's just how it's done here

text: The boss takes the team out for a two-hour lunch. The locals fret about work; for the first time in a year you eat without rushing.
In the evening Ingrid writes from her new office: "Everything's strange. The turnstile won't let me in. How are you?" You laugh out loud.
You're sent on a trip to Ingrid's new office. She meets you at the airport with a sign bearing your name — misspelled.
left: Take a photo with the sign

text: In Ingrid's office everyone takes off their shoes at the door and walks around in socks. Today you're wearing odd socks, one with a hole.
Over dinner Ingrid admits she misses the old office, and you: "I never had a better newcomer." You don't know what to say.
This morning you can't buy coffee: the machine only takes a local app. You stand there remembering the hot milk of year one.
Ingrid asks you to help her new team with onboarding — essentially to give your workshop again, in a third language.
Back from the trip, the turnstile opens first time for the first time ever. The guard applauds.
You receive a fine for sorting rubbish wrong. The letter includes a photo of your bag, zoomed in on a receipt bearing your name.
You talk to a client in the local language for half an hour. At the end he admits he's a foreigner too and understood half.
For the third night running you wake at 4 a.m. to check if anyone at home has written. Nobody has — they're asleep.
left: Ban the phone from the bedroom

text: The bus is twenty minutes late and locals are filing complaints right at the stop. You wait calmly and realise you're not fully local yet.
Rumour has it your team will be disbanded after Ingrid's departure. The new manager's silent; your team is asking you.
An evening email from the manager: "Come see me tomorrow at 9." No subject, no emoji. You're awake till two.
At 9 the manager says he wants to expand your team and put you in charge of a new area. He just writes emails without emojis.
You need to hire two people. CVs arrive from twenty countries. One candidate is from your home town and went to your school.
Reading CV number forty, you realise you're looking for people like yourself a year ago. Whether that's good or bad, you can't tell.
left: Get a colleague to weigh in

text: The candidate is so nervous he knocks a glass of water onto your laptop. The laptop survives; the candidate barely does.
Two finalists: an experienced local and a talented newcomer from abroad with no local language. The manager says it's your call.
right: Hire the newcomer and train him

text: Tonight you must write to the runner-up. You remember getting such letters yourself a year ago and redraft it five times.
Your new hire arrives for day one. The turnstile won't let him in. You meet him with a spare badge and a checklist.
right: Hand over the checklist and run

text: The newbie asks about the purple bread in the canteen. You tell him it's the best bread in the world. A year ago it scared you.
right: Recommend it and get back to work

text: In the evening you tell Mom you now lead a team from five countries. Mom asks whether you're eating soup.
The newbie asks when it gets easier. You answer honestly: "In a year it'll be funny." He doesn't believe you.
Head office announces cuts: you must trim your team's spend by 20%. The first thing suggested is language classes.
In the evening you hunt for other cuts. Two options: the coffee machine, or your work trip home over the holidays.
The coffee machine is taken away in the morning. The team stands in the corridor with mugs as if at a funeral. Olusegun brings a stovetop pot from home.
left: Chip in for a new one

text: In the global chat, a colleague from another office writes dismissively about the countries staff come from. Nobody responds.
Sorting email tonight, you find an unopened message from a year ago: an invitation to your own welcome lunch.
left: Laugh and forward it to the team

text: Your tram stalls at a broken signal. You text the team, in flawless local language, that you'll be late. Nobody notices but you.
right: Grab a scooter and make it

text: One of your team is leaving for better pay elsewhere. He apologises and says he learned a lot from you.
At the leaving do you give a toast in the local language. Someone whispers: "Barely an accent." You're pleased and a little sad.
In the morning there's his empty desk. The manager wants the vacancy filled in two weeks. Hiring here usually takes three months.
Your team of four is doing five people's work. The manager asks if everything's OK. You've learned to tell the truth here.
In the evening you catch yourself telling the team "don't overwork" while sitting in the office at nine. Ingrid's note glares at you.
You arrive to find the team has finished your task for you "so you can rest". You're touched and a little lost.
Your country's consulate asks you to speak at a meeting for new arrivals: "Tell them how you coped." You're not sure you did.
At the meeting, new arrivals ask the questions you asked a year ago: where's the buckwheat, why is everyone silent, how does the shower work.
Over coffee you read the local paper — no dictionary. It's about the weather, but you even get the joke in the last paragraph.
In a client presentation you proudly drop a local proverb. The client politely corrects you: you swapped the last two words, and it came out rude.
Your second New Year abroad. This time your flat is full of guests from five countries, and your family watches everyone over video.
On New Year's morning, tidying up after the guests, you find gifts with cards in six languages. One is a chocolate turnstile.
The manager asks you to set goals for the year. You write three work ones and one personal: "Don't cry in the lift." He leaves it in.
Your new open-plan neighbour talks loudly on the phone in his language all day. You realise a year ago you called Mom the same way.
left: Ask him to keep it down

text: The new manager refuses your leave for your home holidays: "That's quarterly report week." Ingrid always let you go.
Your family celebrates without you and sends a video. You watch it in the office over the quarterly report.
You discover a colleague from next door mixed up time zones and emailed a client at 3 a.m. their time, flagged "urgent".
Two of your team argue over the team chat language: local or English. Both look at you.
In the evening, the team member who lost the language debate sends you a long message about unfairness. In his native language.
The same team member says he'll quit unless the chat goes bilingual. A bilingual chat means twice the messages.
The new manager takes you to lunch and asks if you'd transfer to head office. "More opportunities there — but starting over."
In the evening you take the suitcase down just to look at it. The cat immediately lies inside in protest.
In the morning Gabriela spots the suitcase in your hallway and sadly asks: "Are you leaving?" You don't know yourself.
You ring Ingrid for advice. She says: "Move when you want to go there, not when you want to leave here."
In the evening you list the pros and cons of moving to head office. The item "cat" outweighs five "career" items.
In the morning you tell the manager you're staying. He's unexpectedly pleased: "I was afraid you'd say yes. Who'd translate the locals for me?"
Colleagues explain that on the Friday before a holiday everyone leaves at lunchtime. The new manager doesn't know and books a meeting for 3 p.m.
The manager holds his 3 p.m. meeting. Only you and he show up. After a long silence he asks: "Is it because of me?"
More snow this morning and the city stops. You know the drill now: work from home, make pancakes, watch the window.
A client from your country insists on speaking only your native language. Your manager wants all calls recorded and understandable to the team.
You post Mom a parcel of local sweets. A month later it comes back: "Addressee not found." She's lived there forty years.
right: Send it with a travelling colleague

text: On the tram you see a lost foreigner with a map and a suitcase. He asks someone for directions and gets no answer.
At an international conference you present in English. The audience spans fifteen countries, and they all laugh at your joke at different times.
left: Wait for the laughter to finish

text: In the hotel after the conference you call Mom, Ingrid and Kwame in turn. Each needs telling which country you're in.
The hotel coffee machine has a menu in the seventh language of your life. You confidently press a button. Hot milk.
At the conference someone approaches and speaks to you in your language. He lives abroad too, elsewhere, and offers you a job.
In the evening you realise a job in a third country sounds both scary and tempting. A year ago you'd just have been scared.
left: Keep the card, just in case
right: Put it out of your mind

text: Back from the conference, the team surprises you: each has learned a greeting in your language. You get six different versions.
The manager tells a joke in his language and only you laugh — it's similar to the local one. The others eye you suspiciously.
Your nephew sends a voice note in your city's language: he's started learning it at school "so I can visit". Twelve mistakes.
At the bank in the morning the clerk asks how long you've lived here. "You talk like a local." She too came from another country.
You notice one of your team stays till 9 p.m. every day. He's new and afraid he'll be fired otherwise. You remember that feeling.
Calling Mom tonight, you catch yourself explaining the local recycling rules with all the zeal the locals once used on you.
The office internet dies in the morning and every call with other continents drops. Local colleagues calmly go for coffee.
It's Ngozi's birthday. By local custom she treats everyone to cake. For the first time you're not surprised and bring her a card in her language.
The landlady raises the rent again. The new figure is nearly what a bigger flat on the outskirts would cost.
Back at flat viewings this morning. This time you understand everything the agent says, including what he leaves out.
The new landlord wants a motivation letter again. You write it in ten minutes in the local language, with a joke about a trumpeter.
You're moving out. Gabriela brings a pie, the trumpeter plays a farewell, the downstairs neighbour silently shakes your hand.
First morning in the new flat on the outskirts. Forty minutes to the office by bike, but the window looks out on a field with cows.
Jorge learns you've moved near him and suggests commuting together. He's late always and everywhere.
The new neighbours are an elderly couple who speak neither English nor your language. They bring eggs from their hens and tell you something at length.
right: Thank them and close the door

text: A herd of cows blocks your commute this morning. The herder waves and shouts something. You're late for the head-office call.
left: Snap a photo and send it

text: You're late to the meeting and explain cows blocked the road. The head-office manager doesn't believe you until you show the photo.
It's so quiet out here at night you can hear your thoughts. Your thoughts, it turns out, are in the local language.
The neighbours' hens wander your yard in the morning. One walks in the open door and sits on your work laptop.
The office cleaner is new, from another country, with no local language. She's afraid to ask which rubbish goes where.
right: Put picture signs over the bins

text: The neighbours invite you to dinner. They speak only the local language, and for the first time you understand everything all evening — and even crack jokes.
The village bus runs three times a day. The morning one left two minutes early. Next one's at lunchtime.
The company introduces hybrid work: three days in the office, two at home. Your team wants it the other way round.
You show your parents the new house, the field and the cows. Dad says: "Now I see why you stayed" — and laughs.
The company newsletter names you an "example of successful integration". Below is your first-day photo at the turnstile.
left: Ask them to swap the photo

text: Colleagues joke that you're now "the newsletter star" and want an autograph on a cup. A newbie asks if you really cried in the lift.
You discover someone drinking from your cat mug. It's a new hire who doesn't know the kitchen rules yet.
right: Stick a name label on it

text: A client from another country complains your team's replies are "too short and cold". That's the local style you worked so hard to learn.
Mom has signed up for an online course in the local language "to understand your colleagues". She calls in the evening with homework.
A new local colleague asks where you're from and doesn't believe the answer: "I thought you were from the next district." You blush with pride.
HR asks you to translate the company handbook into your language for a new hire. It's ninety pages, and he starts Monday.
Mustard alone in the fridge again tonight. You smile: a year ago it was a tragedy; now you know where the late-night shop is.
right: Order dinner for you and friends

text: Your bike has a flat this morning. You can fix it yourself now, but it takes twenty minutes and the meeting's in thirty.
left: Fix it and just make it

text: Colleagues forgot Lennart's birthday. He sits alone, pretending not to notice. You know how that feels.
left: Rustle up a cake in an hour

text: An evening call with an office where it's morning. Someone asks, "Is it really dark there already?" You point the camera at the dark window and the stars.
Foggy again this morning, but you don't get lost now: you could find the office blindfold. On the way you meet a newcomer looking for it.
Your team writes you anonymous feedback. The most common comment: "Apologises too much." You apologise in your head.
Hana writes from her home country: "Everything's changed, I feel like a foreigner at home." You understand her better than you'd like.
left: Support her with a long call

text: The cat has learned to open the balcony door and goes off to visit the neighbours' hens. You search the yard in pyjamas every morning.
right: Ask the neighbours to keep watch

text: A courier brings a parcel from Mom. Your address is on the box in her handwriting, in the local language, without a single mistake. You nearly cry.
The elderly neighbours teach you a local card game. You understand the rules, but they still win and are delighted.
The manager asks whether you'd take on onboarding for all company newcomers. A promotion — and a lot more turnstiles in your life.
Your newcomer complains a local colleague is rude in chat. You read the thread: he's just writing briefly, local-style.
left: Explain the style to the newbie

text: Ingrid calls late in the evening: her new turnstile finally lets her through. She's thrilled and wanted to tell you first.
For the first time, your newcomer shows up to the meeting five minutes early instead of on the dot. You're proud as a parent.
left: Praise him in front of all

text: Your team finally eats lunch together instead of at their desks. Five countries at one table, all arguing whose soup is best.
A friend tells you tonight that your favourite café back home has closed. You celebrated every birthday there. You can't even go and say goodbye.
Back at immigration to renew your papers. The officer recognises you: "Oh, it's you! Missing one form again?"
The next department complains your team is noisy: at lunch you teach each other songs. The manager asks you to "find a balance".
Your brother rings: he's got a job abroad — in your country. He wants to stay with you for the first six months.
Your brother lands and confidently delivers a phrasebook line to the taxi driver. The driver gives him the same look he once gave you.
Your brother calls from his new office: the turnstile won't let him in and the guard's gone for coffee. You laugh so hard the whole team turns round.
Tonight your brother moans about everything: the food, the weather, the silent buses. You hear yourself a year ago and start defending the city.
You find your brother's phrasebook on the kitchen table, open at the elephant-at-the-opera page. He's underlined it twice.
left: Leave him a list of real phrases

text: Your brother needs advice: his boss asked whether he wants "direct or very direct feedback". You laugh for a long time before answering.
Mom now calls you and your brother at once and insists you check he's eating soup. He insists you don't.
Monday morning. Forty emails, twenty chat questions, six calls in four time zones. A year ago you'd have been lost.
right: Start with coffee and a walk

text: Head office moves a key meeting to 6 a.m. your time because "it suits everyone else". Everyone else is twenty people.
A friend back home is hurt you missed his wedding for work. You watched the stream at 5 a.m., but he doesn't believe you.
right: Promise to come for the anniversary

text: Translating a local partner's letter for your manager, you missed the word "not". The manager has already replied: "Great, it's a deal."
One of your team admits he wants to go home: the homesickness is too much. He's your best person.
right: Offer to let him work remotely

text: Your brother's off on a work trip and the flat is quiet again. You catch yourself missing his moans about the weather.
You overslept: the alarm was set to home-town time. The meeting's in twenty minutes, the office forty away.
right: Message honestly that you'll be late

text: A new local department head calls your plan "naive" in front of everyone. Locally that's just an opinion. Inside, you're wincing.
Tonight you realise that for three weeks you've been nowhere but office and home. You've only seen the cow field through the window.
No hot water this morning: the village boiler has to be switched on the night before. You forgot, and there's a 9 a.m. video meeting.
right: Go to the meeting as you are

text: You find a mistake in a newcomer's report that's already gone to head office. If you flag it, he'll face tighter checks.
Mom calls for no reason, at a time that suits you. You realise she's learned your time difference by heart too.
In the morning you get a new badge with a new photo. You're smiling not "unacceptably joyfully" but the local way — just a little.
right: Ask for a retake with a big grin

text: A newcomer asks if you regret moving. You stay silent a long time — normal here — then answer: "Sometimes. But never completely."
Friday evening. Colleagues invite you out, your brother to dinner, Mom to a video call and the cat to the sofa. You've energy for one.
right: Stay on the sofa with the cat

text: Monday morning. The turnstile lets you through first time, you greet the guard in the local language and pour yourself coffee, not hot milk.
